title: Rare events and the zero-hit bound
observe: With p = 0.0002 and 8,192 replicates, the run often shows 0, 1 or 2 hits. After 0 hits, the CLT interval is the point 0, and it does not contain p. The exact zero-hit bound 1 − 0.05^(1/n), about 3/n, stays valid. Increase the number of replicates n. Then the width of the Wilson interval decreases.
dsl:
title: Rare events and the zero-hit bound
problem: How many draws show a rare event, and what does a run with no hits tell?
param p = 0.0002 "probability of the event in one draw"
X ~ bernoulli(p = p) "indicator of the event"
prob hit = X == 1 "probability of the event"
focus X

title: A third server or a second power feed?
decision: Decision: install a third server, or a second power feed. Estimated quantity: the daily outage probability θ = P(down = 1) for each alternative.
reason: On one day, each fault either occurs or does not, so each fault is a Bernoulli variable. A common power fault C stops all servers at once. This is the shared-cause idea of the beta-factor model in reliability work.
inputs: pc = 0.0005 and pf = 0.01 per day are illustrative values. The unit is a probability for each day. There is no data. The model assumes identical, independent days.
dependence: C acts on every server. Given C = 0, the faults A, B and T are independent. Thus all dependence comes from the one shared cause.
method: Independent draws of the 4 indicators in each replicate. The estimator is the fraction of replicates with an outage. All alternatives use the same streams, so the paired differences usually have a smaller variance than with independent streams.
diagnostics: The Wilson interval, and the exact zero-hit bound when a run has no outage. The enumeration of the 16 joint states gives the exact reference. Other candidate models: fault times with repair times, and server faults that depend on the load.
interpretation: The second power feed lowers the outage probability most, because the common fault dominates. A third server acts only on the small term pf². It does not change the larger term pc. Reject the model if outages cluster on consecutive days, or if server faults correlate without a power fault.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: A third server or a second power feed?
problem: A service runs on redundant servers. One shared power feed can stop all servers at once. Find the change that gives the lower daily outage probability.
param pc = 0.0005 "daily probability of a common power fault"
param pf = 0.01 "daily probability of an independent fault of one server"
param third = 0 "1 when a third server is installed"
C ~ bernoulli(p = pc) "common power fault"
A ~ bernoulli(p = pf) "fault of server A"
B ~ bernoulli(p = pf) "fault of server B"
T ~ bernoulli(p = pf) "fault of the third server, if installed"
down := C or (A and B and (third == 0 or T)) "the service stops"
prob outage = down == 1 "daily outage probability"
alt "2 servers": third = 0
alt "3 servers": third = 1
alt "2 servers and a second power feed": third = 0; pc = 0.00005
minimise outage
focus down

title: Screen, treat everyone, or treat no one?
decision: Decision: treat after a positive test, treat everyone, or treat no one. Estimated quantity: the expected cost for each person, and the probability of disease after a positive test.
reason: A person has the disease or not, and a test is positive or not. Both are Bernoulli variables. The test result depends on the disease state through the sensitivity and the specificity.
inputs: Prevalence 0.02, sensitivity 0.9 and specificity 0.95 are illustrative values. Costs are in cost units: 1 for one treatment, 40 for one untreated case. There is no data.
dependence: T depends on D: P(T = 1 | D = 1) = sens and P(T = 1 | D = 0) = 1 − spec. Different people are independent.
method: Independent draws of D, then of T given D. The cost estimator is a sample mean. The probability of disease after a positive test is a ratio of 2 means, with a delta-method interval.
diagnostics: CLT intervals for the costs, which have finite bounds. The paired differences compare the policies on the same people. Other candidate models: a prevalence with its own uncertainty, and test errors that depend on the stage of the disease.
interpretation: With these values, the policy that treats after a positive test costs about 0.15 cost units for each person. No treatment costs 0.8, and treatment of everyone costs 1. Only about 27 % of positive tests come from a person with the disease. Reject the model if the sensitivity or the specificity differs between groups of patients.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: Screen, treat everyone, or treat no one?
problem: A test detects a disease with errors. Find the policy with the least expected cost for each person.
param prev = 0.02 "prevalence of the disease"
param sens = 0.9 "probability of a positive test for a person with the disease"
param spec = 0.95 "probability of a negative test for a person without the disease"
param ctreat = 1 {cost units} "cost of one treatment"
param cmiss = 40 {cost units} "cost of one untreated case"
param policy = 1 "1 = treat when positive, 2 = treat all, 3 = treat none"
D ~ bernoulli(p = prev) "the person has the disease"
T ~ bernoulli(p = if(D, sens, 1 - spec)) "the test is positive"
treat := if(policy == 1, T, policy == 2) "the person gets the treatment"
loss := ctreat*treat + cmiss*D*(1 - treat) {cost units}
mean cost = loss {cost units per person}
ratio ppv = E[D*T] / E[T] "probability of disease after a positive test"
alt "Treat after a positive test": policy = 1
alt "Treat everyone": policy = 2
alt "Treat no one": policy = 3
minimise cost
focus T

title: The vote threshold of a launch abort system
decision: Decision: the number k of sensor alarms that starts an abort. Estimated quantity: the expected cost for each launch, with the probabilities of a false abort and of a missed fault.
reason: Each sensor alarm and the fault itself are Bernoulli variables. Given the fault state, each sensor alarms with a fixed probability.
inputs: P(fault) = 0.001, P(alarm | fault) = 0.95 and P(alarm | no fault) = 0.02 are illustrative values. Costs: 1 cost unit for an abort without a fault, 500 for a launch that continues with a fault.
dependence: The 3 alarms are independent given Fault. They are dependent without that condition, because all of them follow Fault.
method: Independent draws of Fault, then of S1, S2 and S3 given Fault. The cost estimator is a sample mean. The 3 alternatives use the same streams.
diagnostics: The enumeration of the 16 joint states gives exact reference values. The missed-fault probability is rare, so the zero-hit bound matters for a small number of replicates. Other candidate model: a common-mode sensor error, which makes the alarms dependent given Fault.
interpretation: k = 2 gives the least expected cost. k = 1 aborts too often, and k = 3 misses too many faults. A run needs about 10^6 replicates, because a missed fault with k = 2 has a probability near 7 in a million. A smaller run often shows no missed fault, and its cost estimate is then too low. Reject the model if the sensors share a power supply or a software fault.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: The vote threshold of a launch abort system
problem: 3 sensors watch for a fault. The system aborts when at least k sensors alarm. Find the best k.
param pfault = 0.001 "probability of a real fault in one launch"
param pdet = 0.95 "probability that one sensor alarms when a fault is present"
param pfa = 0.02 "probability that one sensor alarms when no fault is present"
param k = 2 {sensors} "number of alarms that starts an abort"
param cabort = 1 {cost units} "cost of an abort without a fault"
param closs = 500 {cost units} "cost of a launch that continues with a fault"
Fault ~ bernoulli(p = pfault) "a real fault is present"
S1 ~ bernoulli(p = if(Fault, pdet, pfa)) "alarm of sensor 1"
S2 ~ bernoulli(p = if(Fault, pdet, pfa)) "alarm of sensor 2"
S3 ~ bernoulli(p = if(Fault, pdet, pfa)) "alarm of sensor 3"
abort := S1 + S2 + S3 >= k "the system aborts"
loss := cabort*abort*(1 - Fault) + closs*Fault*(1 - abort) {cost units}
mean cost = loss {cost units per launch}
prob false_abort = abort and not Fault "abort without a fault"
prob missed = Fault and not abort "launch with a fault"
alt "k = 1": k = 1
alt "k = 2": k = 2
alt "k = 3": k = 3
minimise cost
focus abort

title: The law of small numbers
observe: Each alternative keeps the mean np = 3. As n grows, P(X = 0) = (1 − 3/n)^n moves to e^(−3) ≈ 0.0498, the Poisson value. The reference values show the limit. The estimates show the same trend within their intervals.
dsl:
title: The law of small numbers
problem: How close is Binomial(n, 3/n) to Poisson(3) for a small n?
param lambda = 3 "mean count"
param n = 10 {trials}
X ~ binomial(n = n, p = lambda / n) {successes}
prob zero = X == 0 "probability of no success"
prob six_plus = X >= 6 "probability of 6 or more successes"
alt "n = 6": n = 6
alt "n = 30": n = 30
alt "n = 1000": n = 1000
focus X

title: How many tickets to sell for a 180-seat flight
decision: Decision: the number of tickets to sell. Estimated quantity: the expected net revenue for each flight, and the probability that at least one passenger loses the seat.
reason: Each ticket holder comes to the flight or not. If the ticket holders act independently with the same probability, the number who come is binomial.
inputs: 180 seats, P(show) = 0.93, a fare of 200 and a compensation of 600 currency units are illustrative values. The airline does not refund the fare. There is no data.
dependence: None in this model: ticket holders are independent. Groups that travel together break this assumption.
method: The inverse transform or independent draws of X. The estimators are sample means. The alternatives use the same streams, so the paired differences usually have a smaller variance than with independent streams.
diagnostics: Exact reference values by enumeration of the 193 support points. The constraint P(any passenger loses the seat) ≤ 0.05 uses the interval, not only the estimate. Other candidate models: the beta-binomial law for groups, and a show probability that depends on the fare class.
interpretation: 186 tickets give more revenue than 180, and they meet the constraint. 192 tickets do not meet the constraint. Reject the model if many passengers travel in groups, because the variance of X is then larger.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: How many tickets to sell for a 180-seat flight
problem: Some ticket holders do not come to the flight. More tickets than seats raise the revenue, but some passengers can lose their seats. Find the number of tickets to sell.
param seats = 180 {seats}
param tickets = 186 {tickets}
param pshow = 0.93 "probability that one ticket holder comes to the flight"
param fare = 200 {currency units} "fare, not refunded"
param comp = 600 {currency units} "compensation for one passenger who loses the seat"
X ~ binomial(n = tickets, p = pshow) {passengers} "ticket holders who come to the flight"
bumped := max(X - seats, 0) {passengers} "passengers who lose the seat"
mean net = fare*tickets - comp*bumped {currency units per flight}
prob any_bumped = bumped >= 1 "at least one passenger loses the seat"
alt "Sell 180": tickets = 180
alt "Sell 186": tickets = 186
alt "Sell 192": tickets = 192
maximise net
require any_bumped <= 0.05
focus X

title: An inspection plan for parts from a supplier
decision: Decision: the size nsample of the inspection sample and the acceptance number c. Estimated quantity: the probability of acceptance of a good lot (1 % defects) and of a bad lot (8 % defects). The limits: accept at least 95 % of good lots and at most 10 % of bad lots.
reason: A large lot holds many parts, so each sampled part has a defect independently with the lot fraction. Thus the number of parts with a defect in the sample has a law near the binomial law.
inputs: The acceptable quality level 1 % and the limit 8 % are illustrative values. The unit of X is parts with a defect. There is no data.
dependence: None: parts are independent within the sample. The binomial law replaces the hypergeometric law, which is exact for a finite lot.
method: Independent draws of the 2 counts. Each estimator is a fraction of replicates. Sweep nsample or c to see how the probabilities of acceptance change.
diagnostics: The page checks each risk constraint against the interval. Exact references come from the enumeration. Other candidate model: the hypergeometric law for a small lot.
interpretation: No plan with nsample = 50 meets both limits. With c = 1, the plan rejects 8.9 % of good lots. With c = 2, it accepts 22.6 % of bad lots. The plan nsample = 100, c = 3 meets both limits. Reject the binomial model if the sample is more than about 10 % of the lot.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: An inspection plan for parts from a supplier
problem: Inspect n parts from each large lot. Accept the lot when at most c parts have a defect. Find a plan that accepts good lots and rejects bad lots.
param nsample = 50 {parts}
param c = 2 {parts} "acceptance number"
param aql = 0.01 "defect fraction of a good lot"
param ltpd = 0.08 "defect fraction of a bad lot"
G ~ binomial(n = nsample, p = aql) {parts with a defect} "count in a sample from a good lot"
Bd ~ binomial(n = nsample, p = ltpd) {parts with a defect} "count in a sample from a bad lot"
prob accept_good = G <= c "acceptance of a good lot"
prob accept_bad = Bd <= c "acceptance of a bad lot"
alt "n = 50, c = 1": nsample = 50; c = 1
alt "n = 50, c = 2": nsample = 50; c = 2
alt "n = 100, c = 3": nsample = 100; c = 3
minimise accept_bad
require accept_good >= 0.95
require accept_bad <= 0.1
focus G

title: Are Weldon's dice fair?
decision: Decision: keep or reject the fair-dice model for Weldon's dice. Estimated quantity: P(X ≥ 7), the probability of 7 or more dice with 5 or 6, under the fair model and under the fitted model.
reason: One throw of 12 dice gives 12 trials. Each die shows 5 or 6 with probability 1/3 if it is fair. Thus the count of such dice is Binomial(12, p).
inputs: Real data: 26,306 throws, with the counts of dice that show 5 or 6. The fitted p is the maximum likelihood estimate, the mean count divided by 12. The unit of X is dice.
dependence: None in the model: dice and throws are independent. A die with a bias affects every throw, so it changes p and not the independence.
method: Independent draws of X under each alternative. The estimator of P(X ≥ 7) is a fraction of replicates. The data panel compares the observed counts with the expected counts.
diagnostics: The chi-square test of the data against Binomial(12, 1/3) and against the fitted law, with pooled cells. Other candidate model: different values of p for different dice. That model gives the same mean count but a different variance.
interpretation: The fair model fails the chi-square test, and the fitted p = 0.3377 passes it. Dice that show 5 or 6 a little more often than 1/3 explain the data. Do not read the fitted p as the bias of one die, because the data mix 12 dice. Reject the binomial model if the counts spread less than a binomial law allows, because dice with different p give a smaller variance. Also reject it if the counts spread more, because p then changes between throws.
dsl:
title: Are Weldon's dice fair?
problem: W. F. R. Weldon threw 12 dice 26,306 times and counted the dice that showed 5 or 6. Find whether the fair-dice model explains the counts.
param ndice = 12 {dice}
param p = 1/3 "probability that one die shows 5 or 6"
X ~ binomial(n = ndice, p = p) {dice that show 5 or 6}
prob seven_plus = X >= 7 "7 or more dice show 5 or 6"
mean average = X {dice} "mean count"
alt "Fair dice": p = 1/3
alt "Fitted p = 0.3377": p = 0.3377
focus X

title: Labels carry no order
observe: The probability of the rarest category does not change when the labels change order. The mean of the labels changes from 1.75 to 3.25. Thus a mean or a CDF of a categorical law describes the labels, not the law. Compare the alias method with the inverse transform: both give the same law, at a different cost for each draw.
dsl:
title: Labels carry no order
problem: The same categorical law under 2 labellings gives the same probabilities but a different mean.
param w = [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05] "probabilities of the categories"
K ~ categorical(p = w) {label}
relabel := [4, 3, 2, 1][K] {label} "the same category with the labels in the opposite order"
prob rare = K == 4 "probability of the rarest category"
mean label_mean = K {label} "mean of the labels as numbers"
mean relabel_mean = relabel {label} "mean after the labels change order"
focus K

title: Should the emergency department open an observation unit?
decision: Decision: open an observation unit if more than 10 % of arrivals stay over 8 hours. Estimated quantity: the probability of a stay over 8 hours, and the mean stay.
reason: Each arrival gets one of 5 triage levels. The levels are labels with probabilities, so the level is a categorical variable.
inputs: The level probabilities and the mean stays are illustrative values. The stay is a count of whole hours. There is no data.
dependence: The stay depends on the level: H | L ~ Poisson(stay_L). Arrivals are independent.
method: Independent draws: the alias method for L, then a Poisson draw for H. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates.
diagnostics: Exact reference values by enumeration of the level and the stay. Other candidate model: a continuous stay with a gamma law, or with a lognormal law (group 3). The Poisson count of hours has a variance equal to its mean, which can be too small for real stays.
interpretation: With these values, about 5 % of arrivals stay over 8 hours, so the department does not need the unit. Reject the Poisson stay model if the variance of the stay in one level is larger than its mean.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: Should the emergency department open an observation unit?
problem: Each arrival gets a triage level from 1 (most urgent) to 5. The length of stay depends on the level. Open an observation unit when stays over 8 hours are common.
param w = [0.01, 0.12, 0.40, 0.35, 0.12] "probabilities of triage levels 1 to 5"
param stay = [9, 7, 4.5, 2.5, 1.5] {hours} "mean stay for each level"
param limit = 8 {hours}
L ~ categorical(p = w) {level}
H ~ poisson(lambda = stay[L]) {hours} "length of stay in whole hours"
prob long_stay = H > limit "a stay over the limit"
mean hours = H {hours per arrival}
require long_stay <= 0.1
focus L

title: Does a size guide lower the cost of returns?
decision: Decision: add a size guide to the shop, or not. Estimated quantity: the expected cost for each order. The cost for each return is a second quantity, and it can mislead.
reason: Each order ends in one of 5 outcomes: kept, or returned for one of 4 reasons. The outcome is a categorical variable.
inputs: The outcome probabilities, the costs to process each outcome and the guide cost of 0.1 currency units for each order are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: None: orders are independent. The size guide changes the outcome probabilities.
method: Independent draws with the alias method. The cost for each order is a sample mean. The cost for each return is a ratio estimator.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration of the 5 outcomes. The paired difference between the alternatives uses the same streams. Other candidate model: one order with several returned items, with a multinomial count for each order.
interpretation: The size guide lowers the cost for each order. But the cost for each return increases, because size returns have a low cost, and the guide makes them rare. Thus the cost for each return is the wrong quantity for this decision. Reject the model if the guide also changes the number of orders.

dsl:
title: Does a size guide lower the cost of returns?
problem: Each order is kept or returned for one reason. A size guide changes the mix of outcomes. Compare the expected cost for each order.
param w = [0.80, 0.05, 0.08, 0.05, 0.02] "probabilities: kept, defect, wrong size, changed mind, damage in transit"
param cost = [0, 12, 6, 6, 15] {currency units} "cost to process each outcome"
param guide = 0 {currency units per order} "cost of the size guide"
R ~ categorical(p = w) {outcome}
mean cost_per_order = cost[R] + guide {currency units per order}
prob size_return = R == 3 "a return for a wrong size"
ratio cost_per_return = E[cost[R]] / E[R >= 2] {currency units per return}
alt "No size guide": w = [0.80, 0.05, 0.08, 0.05, 0.02]; guide = 0
alt "Size guide": w = [0.832, 0.05, 0.048, 0.05, 0.02]; guide = 0.1
minimise cost_per_order
focus R

title: Send a ranger after a camera alarm?
decision: Decision: send a ranger after an alarm only if a lynx is more likely than not. Estimated quantity: P(lynx | alarm) for the current and a new classifier.
reason: Each detection is one animal of one species. The species is a label with a probability, so it is a categorical variable.
inputs: The species mix and the alarm probabilities are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: The alarm depends on the species: P(A = 1 | lynx) = hit, and P(A = 1 | other species) = false_alarm.
method: Independent draws of S, then of A given S. The quantity P(lynx | alarm) is a ratio of means.
diagnostics: Exact reference values by enumeration of 8 states. The delta-method interval of the ratio. Other candidate model: detections that are not independent, because one animal can pass the camera several times.
interpretation: With the current classifier, about 61 % of alarms are a lynx. The new classifier gives about 82 %, although it misses more lynx. Reject the model if the species mix changes with the season.

dsl:
title: Send a ranger after a camera alarm?
problem: A camera trap classifies each animal. An alarm marks a possible lynx, a protected species. Find whether an alarm makes a lynx likely enough for a ranger visit.
param w = [0.60, 0.25, 0.05, 0.10] "probabilities: deer, wild boar, lynx, other"
param hit = 0.9 "probability of an alarm for a lynx"
param false_alarm = 0.03 "probability of an alarm for another animal"
S ~ categorical(p = w) {species}
A ~ bernoulli(p = if(S == 3, hit, false_alarm)) "the camera raises an alarm"

alt "Current classifier": false_alarm = 0.03
alt "New classifier": false_alarm = 0.01; hit = 0.85
require lynx_given_alarm >= 0.5
focus S

title: Counts compete for a fixed total
observe: The covariance of the first 2 counts is −n p_1 p_2 = −3, although the categorical draws are independent. The counts share one total. If one category gets a high count, the other categories get fewer draws.
dsl:
title: Counts compete for a fixed total
problem: Category counts in n draws have a negative covariance, because they share one total.
param n = 20 {draws}
param w = [0.5, 0.3, 0.2] "category probabilities"
X ~ multinomial(n = n, p = w) {counts}
mean cov12 = (X[1] - n*w[1]) * (X[2] - n*w[2]) "covariance of the first 2 counts"
prob first_wins = X[1] > X[2] and X[1] > X[3] "category 1 has the largest count"
focus X[1]

title: How many shirts of each size to stock
decision: Decision: the stock of each shirt size for one week. Estimated quantity: the expected number of customers without their size, and the probability of any shortage.
reason: Each of the n weekly sales is one size. If buyers are independent with fixed size probabilities, the size counts are multinomial.
inputs: 200 sales each week and the size probabilities are illustrative values. The unit is shirts. There is no data.
dependence: The counts share the fixed total n = 200, so they have a negative covariance. A model with a random total would remove this link.
method: Each replicate draws the counts one at a time from conditional binomial laws. The estimator of the shortage is a sample mean of a bounded quantity.
diagnostics: The page has no reference value here, because the 1.4 million outcomes exceed the enumeration limit. The CLT interval is valid as n → ∞, because the bounded shortage has a finite variance. Other candidate model: a Poisson total with independent Poisson counts for each size.
interpretation: Compare the alternatives with their paired intervals. 10 extra shirts lower the shortage, at a cost that the model does not include. Reject the model if the weekly total itself varies much.

dsl:
title: How many shirts of each size to stock

param w = [0.15, 0.35, 0.35, 0.15] "probabilities of sizes S, M, L and XL"

X ~ multinomial(n = n, p = w) {shirts}

title: How large must a poll be to name the leader?
decision: Decision: the number of respondents. Estimated quantity: the probability that the poll names the party with the largest true share.
reason: Each respondent picks one of 4 parties. If respondents are a simple random sample from a large population, the counts are multinomial.
inputs: The true shares 38 %, 35 %, 17 % and 10 % are illustrative values. The unit is respondents. There is no data.
dependence: The counts share the total n. Thus X_1 − X_2 has the variance n[(p_1 + p_2) − (p_1 − p_2)^2], larger than for independent counts.
method: Each replicate draws the counts one at a time from conditional binomial laws. The estimator is the fraction of polls that name party 1.
diagnostics: References by enumeration are not available for n ≥ 500. Other candidate models: a design effect from cluster samples, and the non-response of some groups.
interpretation: With a lead of 3 points, 1,000 respondents name the leader in about 86 % of polls. 2,000 respondents meet the 90 % target. Reject the model for quota or online panels, where the sample is not random.

dsl:
title: How large must a poll be to name the leader?
problem: A poll asks n voters to choose among 4 parties. Find the probability that the poll names the true leader.

param w = [0.38, 0.35, 0.17, 0.10] "true shares of the 4 parties"
X ~ multinomial(n = n, p = w) {respondents}
prob correct = X[1] > max(X[2], X[3], X[4]) "the poll names the true leader"

alt "n = 1000": n = 1000

title: Do genotype counts depart from Hardy–Weinberg proportions?
decision: Decision: flag the sample for a departure from Hardy–Weinberg proportions if the p-value is below 0.05. Estimated quantity: the Monte Carlo p-value P(T ≥ t_obs) of the chi-square statistic T.
reason: Under the null model, each person has genotype AA, Aa or aa with the Hardy–Weinberg probabilities (q², 2q(1 − q), (1 − q)²). Thus the genotype counts are multinomial.
inputs: Synthetic counts AA = 58, Aa = 84, aa = 58 from 200 people. The allele frequency estimate is q = 0.5, and the observed statistic is t_obs = 5.12.
dependence: None: the people have no family relation. The counts share the total n.
method: Independent draws of the counts under the null model with q = 0.5. In each replicate, a new estimate of q replaces the true q, as for the observed statistic. The p-value estimator is the fraction of replicates with T ≥ t_obs. This is a parametric bootstrap.
diagnostics: An enumeration of all 20,301 outcomes gives the exact p-value of this bootstrap. The chi-square law with 1 degree of freedom gives 0.024. A version that keeps q fixed gives about 0.08, near the chi-square law with 2 degrees of freedom, because it ignores the estimation of q. Other candidate method: the exact test that conditions on the allele counts (Wigginton, Cutler and Abecasis 2005).
interpretation: The p-value is near 0.025, so the page flags the sample. The sample has 84 heterozygotes, against 100 under the model. The bootstrap uses the estimate of q in place of the unknown q, so the p-value is approximate. Reject the Hardy–Weinberg model at the 5 % level when the p-value is below 0.05. Attribute the departure to population structure or relatedness only with other evidence.

data.text: Synthetic: the counts are the expected counts of a model with inbreeding coefficient F = 0.16 and allele frequency 0.5. No random draw made them. The model gives the probabilities (0.29, 0.42, 0.29).

dsl:
title: Do genotype counts depart from Hardy–Weinberg proportions?
problem: A sample of 200 people has genotype counts AA, Aa and aa. Find a Monte Carlo p-value for the chi-square statistic under Hardy–Weinberg proportions.
param n = 200 {people}
param q = 0.5 "allele frequency of A, estimated from the sample"
param t_obs = 5.12 "chi-square statistic of the observed counts"
X ~ multinomial(n = n, p = [q^2, 2*q*(1 - q), (1 - q)^2]) {people}
qhat := (2*X[1] + X[2]) / (2*n) "allele frequency estimated from the replicate"
E1 := n*qhat^2 {people} "expected count of AA"
E2 := n*2*qhat*(1 - qhat) {people} "expected count of Aa"
E3 := n*(1 - qhat)^2 {people} "expected count of aa"
stat := if(E1 > 0, (X[1] - E1)^2/E1, 0) + if(E2 > 0, (X[2] - E2)^2/E2, 0) + if(E3 > 0, (X[3] - E3)^2/E3, 0) "chi-square statistic"
prob pvalue = stat >= t_obs "Monte Carlo p-value"
mean stat_mean = stat "mean of the statistic"
focus X[2]

title: The sum of 2 dice
observe: Each die is uniform on 1 to 6, but the sum S is not uniform: its PMF is a triangle with its peak at 7. Change the plot to the CDF to see the steps, and to the quantile function to see the inverse steps.
dsl:
title: The sum of 2 dice
problem: The sum of 2 independent discrete uniform values is not uniform. Its PMF is a triangle.
D1 ~ uniform(a = 1, b = 6) {pips} "first die"
D2 ~ uniform(a = 1, b = 6) {pips} "second die"
S := D1 + D2 {pips} "sum of the 2 dice"
prob seven = S == 7 "probability of a sum of 7"
prob twelve = S == 12 "probability of a sum of 12"
focus S

title: A die that protects survey answers
decision: Decision: the number t of die faces on which a respondent answers the sensitive question truthfully. Estimated quantity: the probability that the estimate of the share π is within 0.05, and the disclosure risk P(trait | yes).
reason: A fair die gives each face 1 to 6 with probability 1/6, which is the discrete uniform law. The die hides the answer of each respondent, because the interviewer does not see the face.
inputs: 500 respondents and a true share π = 0.15 are illustrative values. On faces 1 to t the respondent answers truthfully, on face t + 1 says yes, and on the other faces says no.
dependence: The die and the trait of each respondent are independent. Respondents are independent.
method: Independent draws of 500 traits and 500 die faces in each replicate. The estimate is π̂ = (ȳ − 1/6)/(t/6), which has no bias for every t.
diagnostics: No enumeration: each replicate has 1,000 variables. The CLT interval of the quantity within is valid as n → ∞, because the bounded quantity has a finite variance. Other candidate design: the Warner design, where the die selects the question instead of the answer.
interpretation: More truthful faces give a more precise estimate but a higher disclosure risk. With the limit P(trait | yes) ≤ 0.5, t = 4 is the best design here. Reject the model if respondents do not follow the die, for example if they always say no.

dsl:
title: A die that protects survey answers
problem: Each respondent rolls a die in private. On faces 1 to t the respondent answers the sensitive question truthfully, on face t + 1 says yes, and on the other faces says no. Find the best t.
param share = 0.15 "true share with the sensitive trait"
param t = 4 {faces} "faces with a truthful answer"
trait ~ bernoulli(p = share) repeat 500 "the trait of each respondent"
D ~ uniform(a = 1, b = 6) repeat 500 {pips} "the private die face of each respondent"
Y := if(D <= t, trait, D == t + 1) "the answer of each respondent, 1 = yes"
est := (mean(Y) - 1/6) / (t/6) "unbiased estimate of the share"
prob within = abs(est - share) <= 0.05 "the estimate is within 0.05 of the share"
mean mse = (est - share)^2 "mean squared error of the estimate"
ratio disclosure = E[mean(trait*Y)] / E[mean(Y)] "disclosure risk: P(trait | yes) for one respondent"
alt "t = 3": t = 3
alt "t = 4": t = 4
alt "t = 5": t = 5
maximise within
require disclosure <= 0.5
focus D

title: How many bits for random record IDs?
decision: Decision: the size m of the ID space. Estimated quantity: the probability that 2 of 500 new records get the same ID.
reason: A good random ID generator gives each ID from 1 to m with the same probability, which is the discrete uniform law.
inputs: 500 records in one batch. The 3 alternatives use 20, 24 and 32 bits. There is no data.
dependence: None: the IDs are independent draws.
method: Independent draws of 500 IDs with unbiased integers. The estimator is the fraction of batches with a repeated ID.
diagnostics: The approximation 1 − exp(−k(k − 1)/(2m)) gives about 0.112, 0.0074 and 0.000029. For 32 bits, a run often has no hits, so the zero-hit bound is the relevant interval. Other candidate model: a generator with a bias, which raises the collision probability.
interpretation: 20 bits give a collision in about 1 of 9 batches. Only 32 bits meet the limit of 0.001. Reject the model if the generator has a small internal state, such as a 32-bit seed for 64-bit IDs.

title: Which dice make a race last 5 turns?
decision: Decision: the dice rule of a board game. Estimated quantity: the probability that a token reaches square 35 from square 0 within 5 turns.
reason: A fair die gives each face with the same probability, which is the discrete uniform law.
inputs: The target square 35 and the 5 turns are design values. The rules are 2 six-sided dice, or one twelve-sided die, for each turn.
dependence: None: the dice are independent.
method: Independent draws of 5 throws for each rule. The estimator is a fraction of replicates.
diagnostics: No enumeration: the repeated variables have too many joint outcomes. Both rules have a similar mean of 35 and 32.5 squares, but different variances. Other candidate rule: a twelve-sided die with a reroll on 1.
interpretation: 2 six-sided dice keep the probability between 0.45 and 0.55. The twelve-sided die gives a lower mean and a larger spread. Reject the model if players can choose to move less than the dice show.

dsl:
title: Which dice make a race last 5 turns?

param rule = 1 "1 = 2 six-sided dice, 2 = one twelve-sided die"

title: The geometric law has no memory
observe: After s = 5 failures, the probability of at least t = 3 more failures is P(X ≥ 8 | X ≥ 5) = 0.8^3 = 0.512. The probability of at least 3 failures from the start has the same value. The ratio estimator for the conditional probability uses only the replicates with X ≥ s, so its interval is wider.

title: How many retries before the link drops a message?
decision: Decision: the retry limit of a radio link. Estimated quantity: the probability that the link drops a message, and the mean time spent on one message.
reason: Each attempt succeeds or fails with a fixed probability, independently of the earlier attempts. The number of failed attempts before the first success is then geometric.
inputs: P(success of one attempt) = 0.7 and 20 ms for each attempt are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: None in this model. On a real channel, failures come in bursts. A two-state Markov channel (the process group) describes that.
method: Independent draws by a count of failed Bernoulli trials, or by the closed-form inverse transform. The estimators are fractions and means.
diagnostics: Exact reference values: P(X > L) = 0.3^(L + 1). Other candidate model: the Gilbert–Elliott channel with bursts of failures.
interpretation: 5 retries meet the drop limit of 0.001 with the least delay. Reject the model if failures cluster in time, because the drop probability is then much larger than 0.3^(L + 1).

dsl:

param psucc = 0.7 "probability that one attempt succeeds"
param limit = 3 {retries}
param slot = 20 {ms} "time of one attempt"
X ~ geometric(p = psucc) {failed attempts}
prob dropped = X > limit "the message is dropped"

alt "3 retries": limit = 3
alt "5 retries": limit = 5
alt "7 retries": limit = 7

title: Does planned replacement help a relay with a constant fault rate?
decision: Decision: replace a relay after T switch cycles, or only after a fault. Estimated quantity: the long-run cost for each cycle, by the renewal–reward theorem.
reason: If each cycle has the same fault probability, independently of the age of the relay, the number of cycles without a fault is geometric.
inputs: P(fault on one cycle) = 0.0005, a fault replacement of 50 and a planned replacement of 10 currency units are illustrative values.
dependence: None: cycles are independent. Successive relays are independent, which makes the replacements a renewal process.
method: Independent draws of X. The cost rate is a ratio of means E[cost]/E[life], with a delta-method interval.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration up to a neglected mass below 10^-13. Other candidate model: a fault probability that grows with age (wear), for example a discrete Weibull law.
interpretation: Planned replacement only adds cost, because the geometric law has no memory: an old relay is as good as a new one. Reject the model if the fault rate grows with the number of cycles. Then planned replacement can help.

dsl:
title: Does planned replacement help a relay with a constant fault rate?

param p = 0.0005 "probability of a fault on one cycle"
param T = 1000 {cycles} "planned replacement age"
param cfail = 50 {currency units} "cost of a replacement after a fault"
param cplan = 10 {currency units} "cost of a planned replacement"
X ~ geometric(p = p) {cycles without a fault}
life := min(X + 1, T) {cycles} "cycles until the replacement"
cost := if(X + 1 <= T, cfail, cplan) {currency units} "cost of the replacement"
ratio cost_rate = E[cost] / E[life] {currency units per cycle}
alt "Replace at 500 cycles": T = 500
alt "Replace at 2,000 cycles": T = 2000
alt "Replace only after a fault": T = 1000000000
minimise cost_rate
focus X

title: How many visits before a site counts as empty?
decision: Decision: the number of visits v after which a site with no detection counts as unoccupied. Estimated quantity: P(present | no detection in v visits).
reason: If the species is present, each visit detects it with a fixed probability, independently of the other visits. The number of visits without a detection is then geometric.
inputs: Occupancy 0.4 and detection 0.3 for each visit are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: The detection depends on the occupancy Z: an absent species is never detected.
method: Independent draws of Z and X. The quantity is a ratio of means.
diagnostics: Exact references: ψ(1 − d)^v / (1 − ψ + ψ(1 − d)^v). Other candidate model: a detection probability that changes with the weather or the season.
interpretation: After 4 visits with no detection, the probability that the site holds the species is 0.14. 8 visits meet the 5 % limit. Reject the model if the detection probability falls on later visits.

dsl:
title: How many visits before a site counts as empty?
problem: A surveyor visits a site until the species shows. The species may be absent. Find the number of visits after which a site counts as unoccupied.
param psi = 0.4 "probability that the species occupies the site"
param d = 0.3 "probability of detection on one visit when the species is present"
param v = 4 {visits}
Z ~ bernoulli(p = psi) "the species occupies the site"
X ~ geometric(p = d) {visits without a detection}
seen := Z and X < v "a detection within v visits"
ratio present_unseen = E[Z*(1 - seen)] / E[1 - seen] "probability of presence after v visits with no detection"
prob detected = seen == 1 "a detection within v visits"
alt "2 visits": v = 2
alt "4 visits": v = 4
alt "8 visits": v = 8
require present_unseen <= 0.05
focus X

title: Overdispersion against the Poisson law
observe: N and Y have the same mean μ = 4. The variance of N is μ + μ²/r = 12, so the ratio Var(N)/μ is 3, where the Poisson law gives 1. The right tail of N is heavier: P(N ≥ 12) is about 40 times P(Y ≥ 12). Use the log axis on the survival plot.
dsl:
title: Overdispersion against the Poisson law
problem: A gamma mixture of Poisson laws has the same mean as a Poisson law, but a larger variance and a heavier right tail.
param mu = 4 {events} "mean count"
param r = 2 "gamma shape: a smaller r gives more spread"
N ~ negbin(r = r, p = r / (r + mu)) {events}
Y ~ poisson(lambda = mu) {events}
mean dispersion = (N - mu)^2 / mu "Var(N)/μ"
prob tail_nb = N >= 12 "P(N ≥ 12)"
prob tail_poisson = Y >= 12 "P(Y ≥ 12)"
focus N

title: A no-claim discount for drivers with different risks
decision: Decision: the claim count c at which a driver loses the no-claim discount. Estimated quantity: the share of drivers who lose it, under the negative binomial model and under a Poisson model.
reason: Drivers differ in risk. If the claim rate of one driver has a gamma law and the claims are Poisson given that rate, the claim count is negative binomial.
inputs: A mean of 0.8 claims a year and a gamma shape r = 1.5 are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: The gamma rate gives each driver a fixed risk, so the claim counts of one driver in different years are dependent. This model looks at one year only.
method: Independent draws by the gamma–Poisson mixture. The estimators are fractions of replicates.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration. The Poisson model with the same mean gives a smaller share in the tail. Other candidate model: a zero-inflated count for drivers who never claim.
interpretation: With c = 3, about 8 % of drivers lose the discount, against 5 % in the Poisson model. A Poisson model would understate the tail. Reject the model if the spread between drivers changes with the age of the driver.

dsl:
title: A no-claim discount for drivers with different risks
problem: Drivers differ in risk, so claim counts spread more than a Poisson law allows. Find the claim count at which a driver loses the discount.
param mu = 0.8 {claims per year} "mean claim count"
param r = 1.5 "gamma shape of the risk spread"
param c = 2 {claims} "claim count that removes the discount"
N ~ negbin(r = r, p = r / (r + mu)) {claims}
Y ~ poisson(lambda = mu) {claims} "the same mean without risk spread"
prob lose = N >= c "share of drivers who lose the discount"
prob lose_poisson = Y >= c "the same share under the Poisson model"
alt "c = 1": c = 1
alt "c = 2": c = 2
alt "c = 3": c = 3
maximise lose

focus N

title: Surge beds for daily admissions
decision: Decision: the number of beds for daily admissions. Estimated quantity: the probability of an overflow day and the mean excess admissions.
reason: Daily admissions vary more than a Poisson law allows, because the rate itself changes from day to day. A gamma rate gives the negative binomial law.
inputs: A mean of 20 admissions a day and r = 8 are illustrative values. The variance is then 20 + 400/8 = 70.
dependence: This model treats days as independent. Real admissions have weekly patterns and sequences of busy days.
method: Independent draws or the inverse transform from the mode. The estimators are fractions and means.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration. Other candidate models: the Poisson law, which underestimates the overflow, and a model with a weekly pattern.
interpretation: 40 beds probably meet the limit 0.02: the reference overflow probability is 0.019. A run needs about 10^5 replicates to separate the estimate from the limit. Until then the page reports the constraint as not separable. Reject the model if busy days cluster.

param beds = 30 {beds}

title: Treat the fish with the most parasites
decision: Decision: the parasite count t at which a fish gets treatment. Estimated quantity: the share of fish treated, and the share of parasites in treated fish.
reason: Parasites aggregate: most fish carry few and a few carry many. The negative binomial law with a small r is the standard model of this aggregation.
inputs: A mean of 6 parasites and r = 0.8 are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: None: fish are independent. The gamma–Poisson mixture gives each fish its own exposure.
method: Independent draws by the gamma–Poisson mixture. The share of parasites in treated fish is a ratio of means.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration. Other candidate model: a zero-inflated Poisson law, with uninfected fish and a Poisson count for the others.
interpretation: t = 10 treats about 22 % of the fish and removes about 61 % of the parasites. Reject the model if the counts come from fish of different ages, because each age group then needs its own r.

dsl:
title: Treat the fish with the most parasites
problem: A few fish carry most of the parasites. Find a count threshold for treatment that removes most parasites but treats few fish.
param mu = 6 {parasites per fish}
param r = 0.8 "aggregation: a small r gives strong aggregation"
param t = 10 {parasites} "treatment threshold"
N ~ negbin(r = r, p = r / (r + mu)) {parasites}
prob treated = N >= t "share of fish treated"

title: Independent Poisson counts add
observe: T = A + B has the law Poisson(5). The reference P(T ≤ 2) = 18.5 e^(−5) ≈ 0.1247 comes from the enumeration of A and B. The estimate of E[(T − 5)^2] is near 5. This agrees with Var T = E[T] = 5.

title: Independent Poisson counts add

param l1 = 2 {events} "rate of A"
param l2 = 3 {events} "rate of B"
A ~ poisson(lambda = l1) {events}
B ~ poisson(lambda = l2) {events}

title: Was a year with 2 deaths unusual?
decision: Decision: start an inquiry into a corps-year with 2 or more deaths, or not. Estimated quantity: P(N ≥ 2) and P(N ≥ 4) for one corps in one year.
reason: A death by horse kick is a rare event with many soldiers at risk. Many independent rare events give a count with a law near the Poisson law, by the law of small numbers.
inputs: Real data: deaths by horse kick in 10 Prussian army corps from 1875 to 1894, 200 corps-years. The rate estimate is the mean count, 122/200 = 0.61 deaths for each corps-year.
dependence: None in the model: corps and years are independent. If the corps have different sizes, the counts do not have one law.
method: Independent draws of N. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The data panel compares the observed counts with the fitted Poisson counts.
diagnostics: The chi-square test of the data against Poisson(0.61), with pooled cells. Other candidate model: the negative binomial law, if the corps differ in risk.
interpretation: A corps-year with 2 or more deaths has a probability of about 0.13, so such a year is common. Only 4 or more deaths would be rare. Reject the model if one corps shows much higher counts than the others.
dsl:
title: Was a year with 2 deaths unusual?
problem: Bortkiewicz counted deaths by horse kick in Prussian army corps from 1875 to 1894. Find whether a corps-year with 2 or more deaths needs an inquiry.
param lambda = 0.61 {deaths per corps-year} "maximum likelihood estimate from 200 corps-years"
N ~ poisson(lambda = lambda) {deaths}
prob two_plus = N >= 2 "2 or more deaths in a corps-year"
prob four_plus = N >= 4 "4 or more deaths in a corps-year"
focus N

title: A counter that saturates above 10 particles
decision: Decision: the length of one count interval. Estimated quantity: the probability that one interval holds more than 10 particles, which saturates the counter.
reason: Radioactive decays of many independent atoms give a Poisson count in a fixed interval. The rate is constant over the experiment, because the half-life is long.
inputs: Real data: Rutherford and Geiger counted alpha particles in 2,608 intervals of 7.5 s. The rate estimate is 10,097/(2,608 × 7.5 s) = 0.5162 particles each second.
dependence: None: decays in different intervals are independent. The dead time of a real counter breaks this assumption at high rates.
method: Independent draws of N for each interval length. The estimator is a fraction of replicates.
diagnostics: The chi-square test of the data against the fitted Poisson law. Other candidate model: a counter with dead time, which records fewer counts than particles at high rates.
interpretation: Intervals of 7.5 s saturate in about 0.2 % of readings. Intervals of 5 s meet the limit of 0.05 % and keep the most counts in each interval. Reject the model if the activity of the source falls during the experiment.
dsl:
title: A counter that saturates above 10 particles
problem: Rutherford and Geiger counted alpha particles in 2,608 intervals of 7.5 s. A counter saturates above 10 counts in one interval. Find the interval length.
param rate = 0.5162 {particles per s} "10,097 particles in 2,608 intervals of 7.5 s"
param interval = 7.5 {s} "length of one interval"
N ~ poisson(lambda = rate*interval) {particles}
prob saturate = N > 10 "the counter saturates"
mean count = N {particles per interval}
alt "7.5 s": interval = 7.5
alt "5 s": interval = 5
alt "3 s": interval = 3
maximise count
require saturate <= 0.0005
focus N

title: Spare seals for a remote pump station

reason: Seal faults come at random times at a constant rate. The number of faults between 2 deliveries is then Poisson.
inputs: 0.3 faults a week and a delivery every 8 weeks are illustrative values. So are the costs: 2 currency units to keep one unused seal, and 50 for each seal that is not available.
dependence: None: faults are independent. A fault that damages a second seal would break this assumption.
method: Independent draws or the inverse transform from the mode. The estimators are fractions and means of bounded quantities.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration. Other candidate model: a negative binomial demand, if the fault rate changes between periods.
interpretation: 5 seals meet the stockout limit 0.05 with the least cost. Reject the model if faults cluster after a pressure surge.

title: Draws without replacement vary less
observe: X counts the successes in 20 draws without replacement from 50 items. Y counts them in 20 draws with replacement. Both have the mean 8. The variance of X is 4.8 × 30/49 ≈ 2.94, the binomial variance times the finite population correction (N − n)/(N − 1).

title: Draws without replacement vary less
problem: Draws without replacement from a finite population have a smaller variance than draws with replacement.
param N = 50 {items}
param K = 20 {items} "success items"
param n = 20 {draws}
X ~ hypergeometric(N = N, K = K, n = n) {successes} "without replacement"
Y ~ binomial(n = n, p = K / N) {successes} "with replacement"
mean var_without = (X - n*K/N)^2 "variance of X"
mean var_with = (Y - n*K/N)^2 "variance of Y"
focus X

title: How many fish to recapture for a population estimate?
decision: Decision: the size n of the second catch. Estimated quantity: the probability that the Chapman estimate is within 20 % of the true population.
reason: In the second catch, the team takes n fish without replacement from N fish, of which K have a mark. The count of marked fish in the catch is hypergeometric.
inputs: N = 2,000 fish (unknown in the field) and K = 200 marked fish are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: None in the model. Fish that avoid traps after the first catch would break the equal-catch assumption.
method: Inverse transform from the mode, or urn simulation. The Chapman estimate (K + 1)(n + 1)/(X + 1) − 1 is a function of X.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration of the support. The bias of the Chapman estimate is small but not zero. Other candidate model: a population that changes between the 2 catches.
interpretation: A second catch of 400 fish gives an estimate within 20 % in more than 80 % of studies. 100 or 200 fish do not. Reject the model if marked fish die more often or mix poorly with the others.

title: How many fish to recapture for a population estimate?

param K = 200 {fish} "marked fish"
param n = 200 {fish} "size of the second catch"
X ~ hypergeometric(N = Npop, K = K, n = n) {marked fish in the catch}
Nhat := (K + 1)*(n + 1)/(X + 1) - 1 {fish} "Chapman estimate"

title: How many ballots to audit in a batch?
decision: Decision: the number n of ballots to check by hand. Estimated quantity: the probability that the audit finds at least one of 10 misread ballots.
reason: The auditors take n ballots without replacement from a batch of N, of which K are misread. The count of misread ballots found is hypergeometric.
inputs: A batch of 500 ballots with 10 misread ballots is an illustrative case. There is no data.
dependence: None: the audit draws a simple random sample of ballots.
method: Inverse transform from the mode. A binomial count Y with p = K/N shows the error of the binomial approximation.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration. Other candidate model: the binomial approximation Y. It gives a slightly smaller probability, because draws with replacement can repeat a ballot.
interpretation: 150 ballots find a misread ballot with a probability above 0.9. 100 ballots give about 0.89, just below the target. Reject the model if the misread ballots cluster in one part of the batch and the sample is not random.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: How many ballots to audit in a batch?
problem: A batch of 500 paper ballots may hold 10 misread ballots. An audit checks n ballots by hand. Find n so that the audit finds at least one misread ballot.
param N = 500 {ballots}
param K = 10 {ballots} "misread ballots in the batch"
param n = 100 {ballots} "ballots checked by hand"
X ~ hypergeometric(N = N, K = K, n = n) {misread ballots found}
Y ~ binomial(n = n, p = K / N) {misread ballots found} "the binomial approximation"
prob found = X >= 1 "the audit finds a misread ballot"
prob found_binomial = Y >= 1 "the same probability under the binomial approximation"
alt "n = 50": n = 50
alt "n = 100": n = 100
alt "n = 150": n = 150
require found >= 0.9
focus X

title: How many lands in a 60-card deck?
decision: Decision: the number of land cards in a 60-card deck. Estimated quantity: the probability of a first hand of 7 cards with 2 to 4 lands. At most 10 % of hands can have 5 or more lands.
reason: A shuffled deck gives a hand of 7 cards without replacement. The count of lands in the hand is hypergeometric.
inputs: Deck size 60 and hand size 7 are game rules. The land counts 22, 24 and 26 are the alternatives.
dependence: None: a fair shuffle gives every hand the same probability.
method: Urn simulation of 7 draws, or the inverse transform. The estimators are fractions of replicates.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration. Other candidate model: a rule that lets a player draw a new hand, which changes the law of the kept hand.
interpretation: 26 lands give the highest probability of a hand with 2 to 4 lands, 0.78, but too many hands with 5 or more lands. 24 lands give almost the same value, 0.77, and meet the limit. Reject the model if the players do not shuffle the deck well.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: How many lands in a 60-card deck?
problem: A deck has 60 cards. A first hand has 7 cards. Find the number of land cards that makes a hand with 2 to 4 lands likely.
param deck = 60 {cards}
param lands = 24 {cards}
param hand = 7 {cards}
X ~ hypergeometric(N = deck, K = lands, n = hand) {lands in the hand}
prob keepable = X >= 2 and X <= 4 "a hand with 2 to 4 lands"
prob flood = X >= 5 "a hand with 5 or more lands"
alt "22 lands": lands = 22
alt "24 lands": lands = 24
alt "26 lands": lands = 26
maximise keepable
require flood <= 0.1
focus X

title: An infinite mean stops the law of large numbers
observe: For the zeta law with s = 1.8, E[X] is infinite. The sample mean tends to ∞, so it has no finite limit. It increases in a step each time a very large rank appears. The page shows no interval and no reference value, because no finite mean exists.
dsl:
title: An infinite mean stops the law of large numbers
problem: For the zeta law with s ≤ 2 the mean is infinite, so the sample mean grows without limit.
param s = 1.8 "tail exponent"
X ~ zipf(s = s, N = inf) {rank}
mean average = X {rank} "sample mean of X"
prob big = X > 1000 "P(X > 1000)"
focus X

title: How large should a web cache be?
decision: Decision: the number C of pages in the cache. Estimated quantity: the hit ratio, the probability that a request finds its page in the cache.
reason: The popularity of a page often falls with its rank as a power law. A Zipf law with exponent near 1 is a standard model of web requests.
inputs: 10,000 pages and the exponent s = 0.9 are illustrative values. The cache holds the C most popular pages.
dependence: None: requests are independent. Real requests show bursts of repeated pages, which help a cache.
method: Inverse transform with a CDF table. The estimator is the fraction of requests with X ≤ C.
diagnostics: Exact references: H(C, s)/H(N, s). Other candidate model: popularity that changes over time, which needs a cache that adapts.
interpretation: 1,000 pages give a hit ratio near 0.67 and meet the target 0.6. 500 pages give about 0.59. Reject the model if the exponent varies between days, because the hit ratio depends strongly on s.

dsl:
title: How large should a web cache be?
problem: Requests follow a Zipf popularity law over 10,000 pages. The cache holds the C most popular pages. Find a C with a hit ratio of at least 0.6.
param s = 0.9 "Zipf exponent"
param pages = 10000 {pages}
param C = 1000 {pages} "pages in the cache"
X ~ zipf(s = s, N = pages) {page rank}
prob hit = X <= C "the request finds its page in the cache"
alt "C = 100": C = 100
alt "C = 500": C = 500
alt "C = 1000": C = 1000
require hit >= 0.6
focus X

title: How large must the dictionary of a spell checker be?
decision: Decision: the number D of words in the dictionary of a spell checker. Estimated quantity: the probability that a message of 300 words holds more than 30 words outside the dictionary.
reason: Word frequencies in text fall with rank roughly as a power law with exponent near 1 (Zipf's law of word frequencies).
inputs: A vocabulary of 50,000 ranks and the exponent s = 1.1 are illustrative values. A message has 300 words.
dependence: This model draws the 300 words independently. In real text, words repeat and follow topics, so the words are not independent.
method: Inverse transform with a CDF table for each of the 300 words. The estimator is a fraction of messages.
diagnostics: No enumeration: each message has 300 variables. Other candidate model: a topic model in which the rank law changes from message to message.
interpretation: Only the dictionary of 20,000 words keeps messages with more than 30 unknown words below 5 %. Even then a message holds about 14 unknown words, because the Zipf tail is long. Reject the independence assumption for long texts, where words repeat.

dsl:
title: How large must the dictionary of a spell checker be?
problem: Word ranks in text roughly follow a Zipf law. A message has 300 words. Find the dictionary size D so that few messages hold more than 30 unknown words.
param s = 1.1 "Zipf exponent of word ranks"
param vocab = 50000 {words}
param D = 5000 {words} "words in the dictionary"
W ~ zipf(s = s, N = vocab) repeat 300 {word rank}
unknown := sum(W > D) {words} "words outside the dictionary"
prob many_unknown = unknown > 30 "more than 30 unknown words"
mean unknown_mean = unknown {words per message}
alt "D = 2,000": D = 2000
alt "D = 5,000": D = 5000
alt "D = 20,000": D = 20000
require many_unknown <= 0.05
focus W

title: Server capacity for viral posts
decision: Decision: plan capacity for posts with more than 10,000 shares. Estimated quantity: P(X > 10,000) for one post, and the mean number of shares.
reason: Share counts of posts have a power-law tail. The zeta law is the discrete law with P(X = k) proportional to k^(−s) on all positive integers.
inputs: The tail exponents s = 2.3 and s = 2.1 are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: None: posts are independent in this model. Real shares spread through a network, which the branching processes of the process group describe.
method: Rejection from a Pareto proposal (Devroye). The tail probability estimator is a fraction of replicates. The mean estimator is a sample mean.
diagnostics: The mean is finite for s > 2, but the variance is infinite for s ≤ 3. Thus the page gives no CLT interval for the mean. The tail probability has an exact reference from the Hurwitz zeta function. Other candidate model: a lognormal law, which has all moments.
interpretation: About 3 in a million posts pass 10,000 shares when s = 2.3. A small change of s changes this probability several times. Plan from the tail probability and its sensitivity to s, not from the mean. Reject the model if the real counts have a tail that decays faster.

dsl:
title: Server capacity for viral posts
problem: The number of shares of a post follows a power law. Plan capacity for the rare post with more than 10,000 shares.
param s = 2.3 "tail exponent of the zeta law"
X ~ zipf(s = s, N = inf) {shares}
prob viral = X > 10000 "a post with more than 10,000 shares"
mean average = X {shares per post}
alt "s = 2.3": s = 2.3
alt "s = 2.1": s = 2.1
focus X

title: Monte Carlo integration of a quarter circle
observe: The estimate of area is near the reference π/4 ≈ 0.7854 from quadrature, and low is near 0.3. The interval of area has a width of about 0.014 with 4,096 replicates, 0.0069 with 16,384 and 0.0034 with 65,536. So 4 times more replicates halve the width, because the standard error falls as 1/√n. The height sqrt(1 − U²) is smooth and decreases in U, so both stratification and antithetic pairs help. With stratification in 16 strata of U, the variance ratio of area is about 75, and antithetic variables give about 3.6.
dsl:
title: Monte Carlo integration of a quarter circle
problem: The mean height sqrt(1 − U²) of a uniform point U on (0, 1) is the area of a quarter of the unit disc, π/4. Estimate it with one uniform draw for each replicate.
U ~ cuniform(a = 0, b = 1) "a uniform point between 0 and 1"
mean area = sqrt(1 - U^2) "height of the quarter circle at U"
prob low = U < 0.3 "P(U < 0.3)"
focus U

title: Which transit line takes a rider to work in the least time?
decision: Decision: the line that a rider takes to work. Estimated quantity: the mean time from the arrival at the stop to the destination, and the probability that the rider is late.
reason: The vehicles of one line leave the stop at a fixed headway. The rider comes to the stop at a time that has no relation to the timetable. The wait until the next vehicle is then uniform between 0 and the headway.
inputs: Headways of 12, 6 and 20 min and ride times of 22, 26 and 16 min are illustrative values. The rider has 33 min before the start of work. There is no data.
dependence: None between the wait and the ride: the ride time is a constant of each line. The model also ignores delays on the road, which would add a second random time.
method: Independent draws of the wait W = headway · U, with U uniform on (0, 1). The estimators are means and fractions of replicates. The alternatives use common random numbers, so one U gives the wait on each line. For the mean time, the variance ratio against independent alternatives is 5 (tram − bus), 8.5 (express − bus) and 2.2 (express − tram). With separate streams each ratio is near 1.
diagnostics: Linearity gives the exact mean time headway/2 + ride: 28, 29 and 26 min. Quadrature gives P(late): 1/12 ≈ 0.083 for the bus, 0 for the tram and 0.15 for the express. Other candidate models: an exponential wait for a line with random departures, and a longer mean wait E[H](1 + CV²)/2 when the headways H vary.
interpretation: The bus has the least mean time among the lines that meet the constraint: about 28.0 min, against 29.0 min for the tram. The express is faster, about 26.0 min, but the rider is late with P(late) ≈ 0.15, above the limit 0.1. The paired intervals separate the bus from the tram. Reject the model if the vehicles come in groups or the rider follows a timetable, because the wait is then not uniform.

dsl:
title: Which transit line takes a rider to work in the least time?
problem: A rider comes to the stop at a random time and waits for the next vehicle. Three lines have different headways and ride times. Find the line with the least mean time that is rarely late.
param headway = 12 {min} "time between two vehicles"
param ride = 22 {min} "ride time to the destination"
param deadline = 33 {min} "time the rider has before the start of work"
W ~ cuniform(a = 0, b = headway) {min} "wait at the stop"
total := W + ride {min} "wait and ride"
mean time = total {min}
prob late = total > deadline "the rider is late"
alt "Bus, every 12 min": headway = 12; ride = 22
alt "Tram, every 6 min": headway = 6; ride = 26
alt "Express, every 20 min": headway = 20; ride = 16
minimise time
require late <= 0.1
focus W

title: Round each invoice line or only the total?
decision: Decision: the rule that rounds the amounts of a 30-line invoice. Estimated quantity: the probability that the buyer rejects the invoice, the mean absolute error of the total, and the mean cost for each invoice.
reason: Each line amount has digits below the rounding step. Prices and quantities vary, so the part below one step is close to uniform. The error of one rounded line is then uniform between −0.5 and +0.5 steps, independently of the other lines.
inputs: The model uses illustrative values: 30 lines and a tolerance of 1 cent in the buyer's match. A rejected invoice costs 12 currency units of manual work. The new layouts cost 0.02 and 0.05 currency units for each invoice. There is no data.
dependence: None: the errors of different lines are independent. Lines that repeat one price, such as many units of one item at a price with 3 decimals, break this assumption.
method: Independent draws of the 30 line errors and of the error of the total, each by a scaled uniform. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. For the first rule, the total error is a sum of 30 uniform values. Its law is the Irwin–Hall law, moved to the mean 0.
diagnostics: The page shows no reference values: the line errors are a repeated variable, and the quadrature does not integrate over 30 copies. For the sum S of 30 line errors, the Irwin–Hall law gives P(|S| > 1) = 0.5289 exactly. The CLT gives about 0.527. Other candidate models: a discrete error on a grid of 0.1 cent, and dependent errors for lines that repeat one price.
interpretation: Round each line fails the constraint: about 53 % of the invoices differ from the buyer's total by more than 1 cent. Its mean absolute error is about 1.26 cents. The page selects Lines to 0.1 cent, with the least mean cost: about 0.021 against 0.05 currency units for Round only the total. Its P(reject) is about 7 × 10⁻⁵. Reject the model if many lines repeat one price, because the errors are then dependent and not uniform.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: Round each invoice line or only the total?
problem: An invoice has 30 lines. Each rounded line adds an error to the total. The buyer's system rejects an invoice whose total differs from its own exact total by more than 1 cent. Find the rule with the least cost.
param step = 1 {cents} "rounding step of each line, 0 if the lines keep all digits"
param round_total = 0 "1 if the total is rounded to the cent after the lines, else 0"
param tol = 1 {cents} "tolerance of the buyer's match"
param rework = 12 {currency units} "manual work for one rejected invoice"
param change = 0 {currency units per invoice} "cost of the new invoice layout"
U ~ cuniform(a = -0.5, b = 0.5) repeat 30 "error of one rounded line, in rounding steps"
V ~ cuniform(a = -0.5, b = 0.5) {cents} "error of the rounded total"
err := step*sum(U) + round_total*V {cents} "error of the invoice total"
prob reject = abs(err) > tol "the buyer rejects the invoice"
mean abs_err = abs(err) {cents}
mean cost = change + rework*(abs(err) > tol) {currency units per invoice}
alt "Round each line": step = 1; round_total = 0; change = 0
alt "Lines to 0.1 cent": step = 0.1; round_total = 1; change = 0.02
alt "Round only the total": step = 0; round_total = 1; change = 0.05
minimise cost
require reject <= 0.02
focus V

title: Which tolerance class fits a shaft to its hole at the least cost?
decision: Decision: the tolerance class of a shaft and its hole. Estimated quantity: the probability that the clearance is outside the functional range, and the mean cost for each pair of parts.
reason: Tool wear moves each diameter at a constant rate between two tool changes, from one end of its band to the other. A part made at a random time then has a uniform diameter on its band.
inputs: The nominal diameter is 20 mm. The bands follow the ISO 286 grades for 18 to 30 mm: IT8 = 33 µm, IT7 = 21 µm, IT6 = 13 µm and IT5 = 9 µm. The shaft band starts 7 µm below the nominal size. The functional range of 8 to 38 µm and all costs are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: None: the hole and the shaft come from different machines, so their diameters are independent. Selective assembly, which pairs large shafts with large holes, breaks this assumption.
method: Independent draws of H and S by scaled uniforms. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. The alternatives use common random numbers, but each class scales the uniforms in a different way. So the variance ratio against independent alternatives stays between 0.99 and 1.2.
diagnostics: Quadrature over the 2 uniform variables gives the reference values. P(misfit) is 0.3795, 0.0183 and 0.0043, and the mean cost is 12.89, 2.55 and 3.03 currency units. The clearance H − S has a trapezoidal law, so these values also have a closed form. Other candidate models: a normal law cut to each band for a centred process, and a triangular law for a process with little tool wear.
interpretation: The fine class IT6/IT5 is the only class that meets the constraint. Its P(misfit) is about 0.004, and its mean cost is about 3.03 currency units. The medium class costs less, about 2.55, but its P(misfit) of about 0.018 is above the limit 0.01. The coarse class scraps about 38 % of the pairs. Reject the model if the diameters gather near the centre of each band, because the misfit probabilities are then smaller.

dsl:
title: Which tolerance class fits a shaft to its hole at the least cost?
problem: A shaft turns in a bored hole. The clearance must stay between 8 and 38 µm. Finer tolerance classes cost more to machine but scrap fewer pairs. Find the class with the least cost for each pair.
param th = 21 {µm} "tolerance band of the hole"
param ts = 13 {µm} "tolerance band of the shaft"
param fd = 7 {µm} "distance of the shaft band below the nominal size"
param cmin = 8 {µm} "least clearance that turns freely"
param cmax = 38 {µm} "largest clearance that stays quiet"
param machine = 2 {currency units per pair} "cost to machine one shaft and one hole"
param scrap = 30 {currency units} "cost of one pair that does not fit"
H ~ cuniform(a = 0, b = th) {µm} "hole diameter above the nominal size"
S ~ cuniform(a = -fd - ts, b = -fd) {µm} "shaft diameter above the nominal size"
clearance := H - S {µm}
prob misfit = clearance < cmin or clearance > cmax "the clearance is outside the functional range"
mean cost = machine + scrap*(clearance < cmin or clearance > cmax) {currency units per pair}
alt "Coarse IT8/IT7": th = 33; ts = 21; machine = 1.5
alt "Medium IT7/IT6": th = 21; ts = 13; machine = 2
alt "Fine IT6/IT5": th = 13; ts = 9; machine = 2.9
minimise cost
require misfit <= 0.01
focus H

title: The normal law and the 68–95–99.7 rule
observe: The estimates of upper and two_sided are near their references 0.1587 and 0.0455, and sq_dev is near σ² = 4. By symmetry, P(|X − μ| ≤ σ) = 1 − 2 × 0.1587 ≈ 0.683 and P(|X − μ| ≤ 2σ) ≈ 0.954. With 3σ the value is 0.997, so the rule reads 68–95–99.7 %. With antithetic variables, the variance ratio of two_sided and sq_dev is 0.50, a loss, and the ratio of upper is about 1.23. The partner X' = 2μ − X gives the same value of an even function of X − μ. So a pair costs 2 evaluations for the information of 1.
dsl:
title: The normal law and the 68–95–99.7 rule
problem: A normal value falls within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of its mean with probabilities near 0.68, 0.95 and 0.997. Estimate two tail probabilities and the variance.
param mu = 10 "mean μ"
param sigma = 2 "standard deviation σ"
X ~ normal(mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
prob two_sided = abs(X - mu) > 2*sigma "P(|X − μ| > 2σ)"
mean sq_dev = (X - mu)^2 "the variance σ² = 4"
prob upper = X > mu + sigma "P(X > μ + σ)"
focus X

title: How many loaves to bake for one day?
decision: Decision: the number of loaves to bake each morning. Estimated quantity: the mean profit for each day, and the probability that the demand is above the stock.
reason: The daily demand is the sum of the purchases of many customers who act independently. By the CLT, such a sum is close to normal when the mean count is large, here 400 loaves.
inputs: The mean demand of 400 loaves and its standard deviation of 80 loaves are illustrative values. So are the price of 3 and the cost of 1 currency unit for each loaf. Unsold loaves have no value. P(D < 0) = Φ(−5) ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁷ is negligible, and the model uses max(D, 0). There is no data.
dependence: None: the model looks at one day. Weather and the day of the week change the mean demand. A separate model for each type of day removes that dependence.
method: Independent draws of D. The estimators are means and fractions of replicates. The control C = D has the exact mean 400. With control variates, the variance ratio of profit is about 3.8 for 400 loaves, 7.4 for 440 and 17 for 480. The ratio is large because profit has a strong correlation with D. With the failure control_mean, the control mean is wrong by 0.1σ, and the estimates move 12 to 20 currency units above their references.
diagnostics: Quadrature over D gives the reference values: mean profit 704.25, 712.53 and 700.00, and P(short) = 0.5, 0.3085 and 0.1587. The closed form E[min(D, q)] = μ − σ[φ(z) − z(1 − Φ(z))], with z = (q − μ)/σ, gives the same values. With the failure control_mean, the estimates are 41 to 105 standard errors from their references at 2^16 replicates. Other candidate models: a negative binomial count for a small bakery, and a gamma demand with a long right tail.
interpretation: Without the constraint, 440 loaves give the largest mean profit, about 712.5 against 704.3 for 400 and 700.0 for 480. The constraint P(short) ≤ 0.25 removes 400 and 440 loaves, so the page selects 480 loaves. The constraint costs about 12.5 currency units of mean profit each day. Reject the model if the sales data show a skewed demand. Reject it also if many days end with an empty shelf, because the stock then cuts the observed demand.

dsl:
title: How many loaves to bake for one day?
problem: A bakery bakes bread each morning before it knows the demand. Unsold loaves have no value. Find the number of loaves that gives the most profit with few days of lost sales.
param price = 3 {currency units} "price of one loaf"
param cost = 1 {currency units} "cost to bake one loaf"
param q = 440 {loaves} "loaves baked"
D ~ normal(mu = 400, sigma = 80) {loaves} "daily demand"
sold := min(max(D, 0), q) {loaves} "loaves sold"
mean profit = price*sold - cost*q {currency units per day}
prob short = D > q "demand above the stock"
alt "Bake 400": q = 400
alt "Bake 440": q = 440
alt "Bake 480": q = 480
maximise profit
require short <= 0.25
focus D
control C = D "demand, with the known mean 400"

title: Does a stack of three parts fit its housing?
decision: Decision: a standard or a precision part C in a stack of three parts. Estimated quantity: the probability that the stack is longer than the housing gap, the mean slack, and the mean cost for each assembly.
reason: Each length is the result of many small independent effects of the machine, the tool and the material. By the CLT, each length is close to normal. The stack length is a sum of independent normal lengths, so it is also normal.
inputs: These values are illustrative: mean lengths of 20, 30 and 50 mm, and a gap of 100.15 mm. The standard deviations are σ_A = σ_B = 0.02 mm, and σ_C = 0.08 mm or 0.03 mm for the precision part. The precision part costs 1.2 currency units more, and one assembly that does not fit costs 30 currency units. There is no data.
dependence: None: the three parts come from different processes. Parts from one batch with the same tool offset have correlated lengths, and the stack variance is then larger.
method: Independent draws of A, B and C. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. Stratification helps only on the variable that drives the variance. With 16 strata of A, the variance ratio for the standard part is about 1.01 for no_fit and 1.06 for slack. A gives only 5.6 % of the stack variance. With 16 strata of C, which gives 89 %, the ratios are about 1.8 and 7.6.
diagnostics: Linearity gives the exact reference of the mean slack, 0.15 mm. The page has no reference for no_fit and cost, because the model has 3 continuous variables. For a sum of independent normal values, P(no_fit) = 1 − Φ(0.15/√0.0072) = 0.0385 for the standard part. For the precision part it is 1.4 × 10⁻⁴. Other candidate models: a worst-case stack of the tolerance limits, and a uniform law for parts from a process with tool wear.
interpretation: The standard part C fails the constraint: about 3.9 % of the assemblies do not fit. Its mean cost, about 1.16, is close to the 1.20 of the precision part. The precision part meets the constraint with P(no_fit) of about 0.00014, so the page selects it. Reject the model if the lengths of part C have heavier tails than a normal law, because the misfit rate then grows.
