title: Up to which main-road flow can side-road drivers enter without a signal?
decision: Decision: the largest main-road flow at which the junction stays without a signal. Estimated quantity: P(a side-road driver accepts the first gap), P(the driver rejects 4 or more gaps), and the mean number of rejected gaps.
reason: Data on gap acceptance often follow a binary logit model: P(accept a gap of length x) = 1/(1 + e^(−(x − μ)/s)). This is the same as a logistic critical gap with location μ and scale s. With Poisson traffic on the main road, the gaps are exponential. So a driver with the critical gap t accepts each gap with probability e^(−q·t).
inputs: A median critical gap of 6 s, a logistic scale of 0.6 s and flows of 400 to 700 vehicles per hour are illustrative values. The limit is 15 % of drivers who reject 4 or more gaps.
dependence: The model takes each driver as consistent: the same critical gap Tc for each gap. Given Tc, the gaps are independent, so the number of rejected gaps is geometric with p = e^(−q·Tc). The drivers are independent.
method: Independent draws of Tc, then of the geometric number N of rejected gaps. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over Tc, with a sum over N, for the probabilities. The mean number of rejected gaps has no reference. N has a geometric law with a random parameter, so the page cannot show that its moments exist. Its value is E[e^(q·Tc)] − 1, which is finite here because q·s < 1. Other candidate models: a log-normal critical gap, and the Cowan model of bunched traffic behind an upstream signal.
interpretation: 500 vehicles per hour is the largest flow that meets the limit. At this flow about 10.7 % of drivers reject 4 or more gaps, and about 44 % accept the first gap. At 600 vehicles per hour the share rises to about 16.4 %, above the limit. Above about 500 vehicles per hour the junction thus needs a signal or another measure. Reject the model if the observed gaps are not exponential, for example in platoons behind a signal.

title: How much reserve to hold against day-ahead load forecast errors?
decision: Decision: the reserve for one hour, from 300 to 750 MW. Estimated quantity: the expected cost of the hour (reserve plus unserved energy), the probability that the error exceeds the reserve, and the expected unserved energy.
reason: The weather changes the size of the forecast error from day to day. A normal error whose variance has an exponential law gives the Laplace law: a sharp peak at 0 and exponential tails. Errors of day-ahead load forecasts often show this shape.
inputs: A Laplace scale b = 100 MW gives a standard deviation of 141 MW. A reserve costs 5 currency units for each MW and hour, and lost load costs 3000 per MWh. These values are illustrative. The limit for P(error > reserve) is 0.01.
dependence: None in this model: it describes one hour only. The errors of adjacent hours have a strong positive correlation, so a shortfall often lasts several hours. A daily model needs a time series of errors.
method: Independent draws of the error. The estimators are the fraction of hours with a shortfall, and the means of the unserved energy and of the cost. The alternatives share the streams, so the paired differences of the cost are precise.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of the error. Closed forms for comparison: P(error > r) = e^(−r/b)/2, and E[max(error − r, 0)] = (b/2)·e^(−r/b). A normal law with the same standard deviation gives P(error > 600 MW) of about 0.00001, against 0.0012 for the Laplace law. Other candidate models: the normal law, and a Student t law for heavier tails.
interpretation: 600 MW gives the least expected cost, about 3,370 currency units for the hour, with P(shortfall) of about 0.0012. 450 MW costs about 3,920, and 750 MW about 3,830. 300 MW does not meet the limit: its P(shortfall) is about 0.025. Reject the model if the history of forecast errors shows a bias, or tails that decrease at a different rate.

dsl:
title: How much reserve to hold against day-ahead load forecast errors?

param b = 100 {MW} "Laplace scale of the forecast error"
param cres = 5 {currency units per MW} "cost of 1 MW of reserve for 1 hour"
param voll = 3000 {currency units per MWh} "value of lost load"

alt "750 MW": r = 750

title: Which privacy budget for a published count?
decision: Decision: the privacy budget ε of a published count. Estimated quantity: the probability that the noise exceeds 5 people, and the mean absolute error.
reason: The Laplace mechanism adds noise with scale Δ/ε to a query with the sensitivity Δ. The ratio of the noise densities at 2 counts that differ by Δ is at most e^ε, so the release has ε-differential privacy. Here the Laplace law is the mechanism itself, not a fit to data.
inputs: A count has the sensitivity Δ = 1, because one person changes it by at most 1. The privacy policy sets the upper bound 1 for ε. The tolerance of 5 people and the limit 0.05 are illustrative values.
dependence: None for one release. Several releases about the same people add their budgets: k releases with ε each give kε-differential privacy.
method: Independent draws of the noise. The estimators are the fraction of releases with an error above the tolerance, and the mean of |noise|. The budget ε is a constant. The alternatives share the streams, so each alternative scales the same draw by 1/ε.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of the noise. Closed forms: P(|noise| > a) = e^(−aε/Δ), and E|noise| = Δ/ε. Other candidate models: the Gaussian mechanism for (ε, δ)-differential privacy, and the geometric mechanism, a discrete Laplace law for integer counts.
interpretation: ε = 0.75 is the smallest budget that meets the limit. Its P(error > 5) is about 0.024, and its mean absolute error about 1.33 people. ε = 0.5 gives P(error > 5) of about 0.082, above the limit. ε = 1 also meets the limit, but it gives weaker privacy. Reject the model if one person can add more than 1 to the count, because the sensitivity is then larger than 1.

title: Which hedge ratio keeps the daily currency loss within a limit?
decision: Decision: the hedge ratio h of a receivable in a foreign currency. Estimated quantity: the probability that the daily loss exceeds 100 thousand currency units, the expected daily loss, and the daily cost of the hedge.
reason: Daily log changes of exchange rates have a sharper peak and heavier tails than the normal law. A normal change whose variance has an exponential law from day to day gives the Laplace law. Its tails decrease as e^(−|x|/b).
inputs: The receivable is worth 20 million in the home currency. A Laplace scale b = 0.004 gives a standard deviation of 0.57 % a day. A hedge costs 0.0001 a day for each unit hedged. These values are illustrative. The daily loss limit is 100 thousand currency units.
dependence: None in this model: it describes one day only. The loss uses the first-order value −(1 − h)·V·R, which is accurate for small daily changes. Volatility clusters make large losses on successive days more likely.
method: Independent draws of R. The estimators are the fraction of days with a breach, and the means of the loss and of the hedge cost. The alternatives share the streams.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of R. Closed forms: P(breach) = e^(−L/((1 − h)·V·b))/2 for the limit L, and E[max(loss, 0)] = (1 − h)·V·b/2. A normal law with the same standard deviation gives P(breach) of about 0.0002 for h = 0.75, against 0.0034 for the Laplace law. Other candidate models: the normal law, and a Student t law.
interpretation: A 75 % hedge is the least hedge that meets the limit. Its P(breach) is about 0.0034, its expected loss about 10 thousand currency units a day, and its cost 1.5 thousand a day. A 50 % hedge gives P(breach) of about 0.041, above 0.01. Reject the model if the daily changes have a trend, or if the tails in the history decrease more slowly than e^(−|x|/b).

title: A finite variance does not make the sample mean behave
observe: For σ = 2.5, E[X] = e^(3.125) ≈ 22.76, but the standard deviation is about 518 and the skewness is about 11,800. All moments exist, so the CLT applies. But it applies only for very large samples. The page runs 64 blocks of 1,024 values. The 95 % CLT interval of one block contains 22.76 in only about 45 of 64 blocks, about 70 %. Most blocks miss the rare very large values. Thus their mean is too low and their interval is too narrow. For σ = 1 the coverage is about 61 of 64 blocks, near 95 %. P(X > 10) is 0.0107 for σ = 1 and 0.179 for σ = 2.5. On the log–log tail plot the survival curve bends down. It is not a straight line, so the tail is not regularly varying.

prob big = X > 10 "P(X > 10)"

focus X

title: When to send a second copy of a slow request?
decision: Decision: the delay d after which the client sends a second copy of a slow request. Estimated quantity: the fraction of requests with a second copy, which is the extra load, and P(latency > 250 ms).
reason: A response time is the product of many independent factors: queue lengths, cache misses and retries. The log of a product is a sum, so the response time is near lognormal. The lognormal law is a standard model of the body of server latency. A second copy cuts the slow requests, because two independent copies are rarely both slow.
inputs: A median response time of 40 ms and σ = 0.8 for the log response time are illustrative values. The latency target is at most 0.3 % of requests above 250 ms. There is no data.
dependence: The two copies go to two servers and are independent. A load peak on all servers breaks this assumption, because then both copies are slow together. The second copy also adds load, which this model does not feed back into the response time.
method: Independent draws of R1 and R2. The estimators are fractions and sample means. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
diagnostics: The extra load P(R1 > d) has an exact reference from the lognormal survival function: 0.306, 0.126, 0.049 and 0.022 for the 4 delays. The late fraction has a quadrature reference: it is P(R1 > 250) P(R2 > 250 − d) for d < 250. With no second copy, P(R1 > 250) = 0.011. Other candidate models: a gamma or Weibull response time, and a lognormal body with a Pareto tail for rare stalls.
interpretation: A delay of 150 ms meets the target with the least extra load. About 4.9 % of requests get a second copy, and about 0.14 % of requests are late. A delay of 200 ms gives 0.43 % late requests, which misses the target. A delay of 60 ms doubles the load of 30 % of requests for a small gain. Reject the model if the slow requests of the two servers occur together, or if the measured tail is heavier than the lognormal tail.

title: Which daily dose for a drug with variable clearance?
decision: Decision: the daily dose of a drug given as a constant infusion. Estimated quantity: P(the mean concentration is in the window 2–6 mg/L) and P(the concentration is above the toxic limit 6 mg/L).
reason: The clearance of a drug differs between patients by factors: body size, liver function and enzyme genes. Population pharmacokinetics models such factors as a lognormal law of the clearance. Then the concentration dose/(24·CL) is also lognormal, because 1/CL is lognormal.
inputs: A median clearance of 5 L/h and a standard deviation 0.35 of the log clearance are illustrative values. The window 2–6 mg/L is also illustrative. The dose is in mg/day, so the dose rate is dose/24 in mg/h. There is no data.
dependence: None: one patient, one clearance. The model ignores the change of the clearance with time and with other drugs.
method: Independent draws of CL. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
diagnostics: Each probability reads only CL, so the page computes a quadrature reference. The exact value is a normal probability: for example, P(C > 6) = P(Z > (log(5) − log(dose/144))/0.35). It gives 0.047 for 400 mg/day. Other candidate models: a gamma law of the clearance, and a covariate model with the body weight.
interpretation: 400 mg/day puts about 88 % of patients in the window, with about 4.7 % above the toxic limit. 500 mg/day puts about 15 % above the toxic limit, which breaks the constraint. 300 mg/day is safe, but about 26 % of patients are below the window. Reject the model if the lognormal law does not fit the skewness of measured concentrations, or if a covariate explains much of the clearance.

title: Which rule to declare a workplace compliant from 6 measurements?
decision: Decision: the rule constant c. A workplace passes if the geometric mean of 6 shift exposures is at most c times the exposure limit. Estimated quantity: P(a bad workplace passes) and P(a good workplace passes).
reason: Occupational exposures between shifts are close to lognormal, with a geometric standard deviation of about 2 to 3. Hygiene standards and their statistical tools use this model. The geometric mean is the natural statistic, because the log values are normal.
inputs: Exposures are fractions of the limit, so the limit is 1. The geometric standard deviation 2.5 is illustrative. A bad workplace has 10 % of shifts above the limit: its true geometric mean is 0.309. A good workplace has 1 % of shifts above the limit: its true geometric mean is 0.119. The rule must pass a bad workplace in at most 5 % of surveys. There is no data.
dependence: The 6 shifts are independent in this model. Shifts of the same worker or the same week are often correlated. Then the geometric mean of the sample varies more, and a bad workplace passes more often.
method: Independent draws of 6 exposures for each workplace. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
diagnostics: The page gives no reference, because the variables repeat. An exact check exists: the log of the sample geometric mean is N(log g, (log 2.5)²/6). It gives P(a bad workplace passes) = 0.0013, 0.027, 0.122 and 0.286 for c = 0.10, 0.15, 0.20 and 0.25. P(a good workplace passes) is 0.321, 0.732, 0.917 and 0.976. The estimate of P(one shift above the limit) in the bad workplace is about 0.10, as designed. Other candidate models: a gamma law of the exposure, and a random worker effect. Other candidate rule: an upper tolerance limit for the 95th percentile.
interpretation: c = 0.15 is the largest of the 4 constants that meets the 5 % limit. A bad workplace passes in about 2.6 % of surveys, and a good workplace passes in about 73 %. c = 0.20 passes a bad workplace in about 12 % of surveys. Six measurements cannot separate the two workplaces better. Reject the model if the log exposures are not near normal, or if the shifts of one worker show a strong correlation.

title: The Weibull shape sets the ageing
observe: All three laws give P(T > 1) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368. The ratio P(T > 2 | T > 1) = exp(−(2^k − 1)) shows the ageing. For k = 0.5 it is 0.661, larger than 0.368: an old unit is better than a new unit. For k = 1 it is 0.368: the exponential law has no memory. For k = 2 it is only 0.050: an old unit wears out. The mean life λΓ(1 + 1/k) is 2 for k = 0.5, 1 for k = 1 and 0.886 for k = 2. On the log survival plot, the curve for k = 0.5 is convex. The curve for k = 1 is a straight line. The curve for k = 2 falls faster and faster.

title: The Weibull shape sets the ageing
problem: Three Weibull laws have the scale λ = 1, so P(T > 1) = e^(−1) for all three. Compare the chance that a new unit survives 1 unit of time with the chance that a unit of age 1 survives 1 more unit.
param k = 1 "shape"
T ~ weibull(k = k, lambda = 1) {years} "life of a unit"
prob new_unit = T > 1 "P(T > 1)"
ratio old_unit = E[T > 2] / E[T > 1] "P(T > 2 | T > 1)"
mean m = T {years} "mean life"
alt "k = 0.5": k = 0.5
alt "k = 1": k = 1
alt "k = 2": k = 2
focus T

title: When to replace a bearing that wears out?
decision: Decision: the age τ at which the team replaces a pump bearing before it fails. Estimated quantity: the long-run cost for each hour of operation, E[cost]/E[min(T, τ)], by the renewal–reward theorem.
reason: The Weibull law is the standard model of the fatigue life of rolling bearings. Wear-out gives a shape above 1. A shape above 1 means a growing hazard. Only then can a planned replacement lower the cost.
inputs: The shape k = 2.5 and the scale λ = 20,000 h are illustrative values. A failure costs 12,000 and a planned replacement 1,500 currency units, also illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: Successive bearings are independent and have the same law, which makes the replacements a renewal process. A misaligned shaft breaks this assumption, because it shortens all bearings on that pump.
method: Independent draws of T. The cost rate is a ratio of two means, with a delta-method interval. The alternatives use the same draws.
diagnostics: The page gives quadrature references for the cost rate, and exact references for P(T ≤ τ). The cost rate is 0.368, 0.323, 0.365 and 0.676 for τ = 5,000, 8,000 and 12,000 h and for no planned replacement. Other candidate models: a lognormal life, and a Weibull law with a minimum life (3 parameters).
interpretation: Replacement at 8,000 h gives the least cost rate of these ages, about 0.323 for each hour. Replacement only after a failure costs about 0.676 for each hour, more than twice as much. At 8,000 h about 9.6 % of bearings still fail before the planned replacement. Reject the model if the life data give a Weibull shape near 1 or below 1. Then a planned replacement does not help.

title: Which site gives more energy from the same turbine?
decision: Decision: the site for a 2 MW turbine. Estimated quantity: the mean power, and the capacity factor E[power]/2 MW.
reason: The hourly mean wind speed at a site is close to a Weibull law, often with a shape near 2. Wind resource assessments use this model. The power is a nonlinear function of the speed, so the mean power needs the whole law, not only the mean speed.
inputs: Site A has k = 2 and λ = 7.5 m/s. Site B has k = 1.6 and λ = 8 m/s. These values are illustrative. The power curve is a simple model. The power is 0 below 3 m/s and above 25 m/s. It increases as a cubic to 2 MW at 12 m/s, then stays at 2 MW. The project needs a capacity factor of at least 0.3.
dependence: The model uses the marginal law of one hour. The mean power needs only this law. The variability of the energy in one year depends on the correlation between hours, which this model does not give.
method: Independent draws of V. The estimators are sample means and fractions. The alternatives use the same uniform numbers.
diagnostics: Each quantity reads only V. Thus the page gives quadrature references. Site A gives a mean power of 0.523 MW and a capacity factor of 0.261. Site B gives 0.622 MW and 0.311. Other candidate models: a Rayleigh law (k = 2), a mixture of two Weibull laws for two seasons, and a measured power curve.
interpretation: Site B gives about 19 % more energy, and only site B meets the capacity factor 0.3. Its lower shape gives more hours above 12 m/s, about 14.6 % against 7.7 %. It also gives more idle hours, about 19 % against 15 %. Reject the model if a year of measured hourly speeds does not fit a Weibull law, for example with two modes.

title: Which design stress for a ceramic part?
decision: Decision: the design stress of a ceramic part. Estimated quantity: P(the part fails), the probability that the weakest of its 20 unit volumes is weaker than the stress.
reason: A brittle part fails at its weakest flaw. Weibull's weakest-link theory gives a Weibull law of the strength. The minimum of n independent Weibull(m, s0) values is Weibull(m, s0 n^(−1/m)). Thus a larger part is weaker.
inputs: The Weibull modulus m = 10 and the scale s0 = 400 MPa for one unit volume are illustrative values. The part has 20 unit volumes under the same stress. The load is 30 kN, and the cross-section is the load divided by the stress. The failure probability must be at most 0.001.
dependence: The flaws in different unit volumes are independent. A processing defect that affects the whole part breaks this assumption.
method: Independent draws of 20 strengths and their minimum. The estimator is a fraction of replicates. A probability near 0.001 needs many replicates, so check the width of the interval.
diagnostics: The minimum of a repeated variable has an exact reference: P(fail) = 1 − exp(−20 (s/400)^10). It gives 0.00012, 0.00055, 0.0021 and 0.0068 for the 4 stresses. A test bar of one unit volume fails at 140 MPa with probability 0.000028, 20 times less. Other candidate models: a lognormal strength, and a strength with a lower bound from proof testing.
interpretation: 140 MPa is the largest stress that meets the limit, with P(fail) about 0.00055 and a cross-section of 214 mm². 160 MPa gives P(fail) about 0.0021, which breaks the limit. A design from test bars alone would ignore the size effect. Reject the model if the test strengths do not lie on a straight line on a Weibull plot.

title: Which design stress for a ceramic part?

param stress = 150 {MPa} "design stress"
param load = 30 {kN} "load on the part"
S ~ weibull(k = m, lambda = s0) repeat 20 {MPa} "strength of each unit volume"
part := min(S) {MPa} "strength of the part: its weakest unit volume"
prob fail = part <= stress "the part fails under the design stress"
prob bar_fail = S[1] <= stress "a test bar of one unit volume fails at the same stress"
mean area = 1000*load/stress {mm²} "cross-section that carries the load"
alt "120 MPa": stress = 120
alt "140 MPa": stress = 140
alt "160 MPa": stress = 160
alt "180 MPa": stress = 180

title: The same mean and variance, different tails
observe: X ~ IG(1, 1) and Y, a lognormal value with σ² = log 2, both have the mean 1 and the variance 1. The tails still differ. P(X > 4) = 0.0209 is larger than P(Y > 4) = 0.0187. But P(X > 8) = 0.00126 is smaller than P(Y > 8) = 0.00178. At 16 the lognormal tail is about 9.5 times the inverse Gaussian tail: 0.0000897 against 0.0000094. The inverse Gaussian tail is exponential, and the lognormal tail is subexponential. On the log survival plot the inverse Gaussian curve becomes a straight line, and the lognormal curve bends up and falls more slowly.
dsl:
title: The same mean and variance, different tails
problem: X ~ IG(1, 1) and a lognormal value Y both have the mean 1 and the variance 1. Compare their tails.
X ~ invgauss(mu = 1, lambda = 1) "inverse Gaussian value"
Y ~ lognormal(mu = -0.5*log(2), sigma = sqrt(log(2))) "lognormal value with the same mean and variance"
prob x4 = X > 4 "P(X > 4)"
prob y4 = Y > 4 "P(Y > 4)"
prob x8 = X > 8 "P(X > 8)"
prob y8 = Y > 8 "P(Y > 8)"
prob x16 = X > 16 "P(X > 16)"
prob y16 = Y > 16 "P(Y > 16)"
mean mx = X "E[X] = 1"
mean my = Y "E[Y] = 1"
focus X

title: How large a protection zone around a drinking-water well?
decision: Decision: the radius L of the protection zone around a drinking-water well. Estimated quantity: P(T < 50 days), the probability that water from the edge of the zone arrives in less than 50 days.
reason: In one dimension, a solute that moves with a mean velocity v and a dispersion D reaches the distance L at a first-passage time. This time has the inverse Gaussian law IG(L/v, L²/(2D)). Hydrogeologists use it for travel-time distributions.
inputs: A mean velocity v = 1 m/day and a dispersivity a = 5 m, with D = a·v, are illustrative values. The 50-day travel time is a common basis for the inner protection zone of a well. The probability limit 0.01 is a choice of this example.
dependence: None for one water particle. The model assumes a uniform aquifer in one dimension. Layers and fractures give fast paths that this model does not have.
method: Independent draws of T by the transformation of Michael, Schucany and Haas. The estimators are fractions and sample means.
diagnostics: T has constant parameters, so P(T < 50) has an exact reference from the inverse Gaussian CDF. It is 0.049, 0.017, 0.0051 and 0.0013 for L = 90, 100, 110 and 120 m. The mean travel time is L/v. Other candidate models: a lognormal travel time, and a model with two flow paths.
interpretation: L = 110 m is the smallest radius that meets the limit, with P(T < 50 days) about 0.005 and an area of 3.8 ha. A radius of 50 m, the mean travel distance in 50 days, would fail often. The dispersion spreads the arrivals, so the zone must be about twice that distance. Reject the model if tracer tests give a breakthrough curve with a long early tail or two peaks.

dsl:
title: How large a protection zone around a drinking-water well?
problem: A common rule assumes that the number of bacteria and viruses in groundwater decreases enough in about 50 days. A protection zone around a well forbids sources of pollution within the distance L. Find the smallest L with a small chance that water from the edge of the zone reaches the well in less than 50 days.
param v = 1 {m/day} "mean groundwater velocity"
param a = 5 {m} "longitudinal dispersivity of the aquifer"
param L = 100 {m} "radius of the protection zone"
param tmin = 50 {days} "die-off time of pathogens"
T ~ invgauss(mu = L/v, lambda = L^2/(2*a*v)) {days} "travel time from the edge of the zone to the well"
prob early = T < tmin "water from the edge arrives in less than 50 days"
mean travel = T {days} "mean travel time"
mean area = 3.14159*L^2/10000 {ha} "area of the zone"
alt "L = 90 m": L = 90
alt "L = 100 m": L = 100
alt "L = 110 m": L = 110
alt "L = 120 m": L = 120
minimise area
require early <= 0.01
focus T

title: How often to inspect a part that wears with a drift?
decision: Decision: the inspection interval of a part that wears. Estimated quantity: the long-run cost for each month, E[cost]/E[cycle], by the renewal–reward theorem. Also P(the part fails before an inspection finds it).
reason: If the wear is a Brownian motion with a positive drift, the time to reach a fixed level is inverse Gaussian. The time to the alarm level and the further time to the failure level are independent, by the strong Markov property. Both are inverse Gaussian.
inputs: A drift of 0.1 mm/month and a standard deviation of 0.15 mm after one month are illustrative values. The alarm level is 1.5 mm and the failure level 2 mm. An inspection costs 100, a planned replacement 1,000 and a failure 10,000 currency units. There is no data.
dependence: The two passage times are independent, as the Brownian model implies. Successive parts are independent, which makes the replacements a renewal process.
method: Independent draws of A and G. Inspections are at dt, 2dt, …. The first inspection after A finds the part. The cost rate is a ratio of means with a delta-method interval.
diagnostics: The page gives no reference: the cost reads two variables, and its quadrature needs too much work. Checks: E[A] = 15 months and E[G] = 5 months are exact. The fraction of failures must grow with the interval. Other candidate models: a gamma wear process, which never decreases, and a random drift for each part.
interpretation: An inspection every 2 months gives the least cost rate, about 127 currency units for each month. About 2.6 % of parts then fail before an inspection finds them. Monthly inspections cost about 165, and inspections every 4 months about 172, with about 17 % failures. Reject the model if the measured wear decreases between inspections more than the measurement error allows. Then the gamma process is a better model.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

dsl:
title: How often to inspect a part that wears with a drift?
problem: The wear of a part grows with a constant drift and random fluctuations. An inspection finds the part if its wear has passed the alarm level, and the part is then replaced. If the wear reaches the failure level before an inspection finds it, the part fails. Find the inspection interval with the least cost for each month.
param drift = 0.1 {mm/month} "mean wear rate"
param vol = 0.15 {mm/sqrt(month)} "standard deviation of the wear after one month"
param alarm = 1.5 {mm} "alarm level of the wear"
param fail_level = 2 {mm} "failure level of the wear"
param dt = 2 {months} "inspection interval"
param cinsp = 100 {currency units} "cost of one inspection"
param cprev = 1000 {currency units} "cost of a planned replacement"
param cfail = 10000 {currency units} "cost of a failure"
A ~ invgauss(mu = alarm/drift, lambda = alarm^2/vol^2) {months} "time until the wear reaches the alarm level"
G ~ invgauss(mu = (fail_level - alarm)/drift, lambda = (fail_level - alarm)^2/vol^2) {months} "further time from the alarm level to the failure level"
found := ceil(A/dt)*dt {months} "first inspection after the alarm"
failed := A + G < found "the part fails before an inspection finds it"
cycle := min(A + G, found) {months} "time until the replacement"
cost := cinsp*floor(cycle/dt) + if(failed, cfail, cprev) {currency units} "cost of one cycle"
ratio cost_rate = E[cost] / E[cycle] {currency units per month}
prob fail = failed "the part fails before it is found"
alt "Every month": dt = 1
alt "Every 2 months": dt = 2
alt "Every 3 months": dt = 3
alt "Every 4 months": dt = 4
minimise cost_rate
focus A

title: Which lead time to quote for a batch of 20 jobs?
decision: Decision: the lead time quoted to the customer for a batch of 20 jobs. Estimated quantity: P(the batch is late) and the expected cost of the quote and the penalty.
reason: A job ends when its accumulated work reaches a fixed amount, and the work rate fluctuates. A first-passage time of a Brownian motion with drift is inverse Gaussian. Sums stay in the family: the sum of 20 IG(μ, λ) times is IG(20μ, 400λ).
inputs: A mean job time of 1 h and a shape λ = 4 h are illustrative values, so the coefficient of variation of one job is 0.5. Each hour of quoted lead time costs 50, and a late batch costs 2,000 currency units. There is no data.
dependence: The 20 job times are independent. A slow operator or a worn tool makes all jobs of a batch slow, which breaks this assumption and makes the batch time more variable.
method: Independent draws of 20 job times and their sum. The estimators are a fraction and a sample mean. The alternatives use the same draws.
diagnostics: The sum has an exact law. Thus the page shows exact references for P(S > quote): 0.181, 0.045, 0.0079 and 0.0010 for the 4 quotes. The expected cost has a quadrature reference. Other candidate models: gamma or lognormal job times. Their sum has no simple closed form.
interpretation: A quote of 24 h has the least expected cost, about 1,291 currency units, and the batch is late with probability about 0.045. A quote of 22 h costs about 1,463 because 18 % of batches are late. Reject the model if the job times of one batch show a correlation. Then the batch time has a larger variance than 20μ³/λ = 5 h².

dsl:
title: Which lead time to quote for a batch of 20 jobs?
problem: A machine does 20 jobs of a batch one after the other. Each job ends when the accumulated work reaches a fixed amount, and the work rate fluctuates. The customer gets a penalty if the batch is late. Find the quoted lead time with the least expected cost.
param mu = 1 {h} "mean time of one job"
param lambda = 4 {h} "shape of the job time"
param n = 20 "jobs in the batch"
param quote = 24 {h} "quoted lead time"
param hold = 50 {currency units per hour} "cost of each hour of quoted lead time"
param penalty = 2000 {currency units} "penalty for a late batch"
J ~ invgauss(mu = mu, lambda = lambda) repeat 20 {h} "time of each job"
S := sum(J) {h} "time to finish the batch: IG(20μ, 400λ)"
prob late = S > quote "the batch is late"
mean cost = hold*quote + penalty*(S > quote) {currency units} "quoted time cost plus the expected penalty"
alt "Quote 22 h": quote = 22
alt "Quote 24 h": quote = 24
alt "Quote 26 h": quote = 26
alt "Quote 28 h": quote = 28
minimise cost
focus S

title: The hazard doubles every 8 years
observe: The hazard starts at 0.001 per year at age 30 and doubles every 8 years, so b = log(2)/8 ≈ 0.0866. The chance to live 10 more years is 0.984 at age 30. It falls to 0.601 at age 70, 0.298 at age 80 and 0.056 at age 90. The mean life after age 30 is e^η E1(η)/b ≈ 45.5 years. On the log survival plot the curve falls faster and faster, because log S(t) = −η(e^(bt) − 1). The ratio estimators use only the replicates that survive to the given age, so their intervals are wider at old ages.
dsl:
title: The hazard doubles every 8 years
problem: An adult has the hazard 0.001 per year at age 30, and the hazard doubles every 8 years. T is the life after age 30. Compare the chance to live 10 more years at the ages 30, 70, 80 and 90.
param h0 = 0.001 {per year} "hazard at age 30"
param b = log(2)/8 {per year} "growth rate of the hazard"
T ~ gompertz(eta = h0/b, b = b) {years} "life after age 30"
prob at30 = T > 10 "P(10 more years at age 30)"
ratio at70 = E[T > 50] / E[T > 40] "P(10 more years | alive at 70)"
ratio at80 = E[T > 60] / E[T > 50] "P(10 more years | alive at 80)"
ratio at90 = E[T > 70] / E[T > 60] "P(10 more years | alive at 90)"
mean life = T {years} "mean life after age 30"
focus T

title: Which anti-ageing intervention to take forward in mice?
decision: Decision: which of two interventions in mice to take forward to a larger study. Estimated quantity: the mean lifespan, and P(a mouse lives more than 1,000 days).
reason: Adult mortality of mice, like that of humans, is close to the Gompertz law over most adult ages: the log hazard grows linearly with age. The two parameters separate two effects. η·b is the initial hazard, and b is the rate of ageing.
inputs: An initial hazard of 0.000014 per day and a doubling time of the hazard of 100 days are illustrative values. They give a mean lifespan of about 814 days. One intervention halves the initial hazard. The other lowers b by 15 % with the same initial hazard, so η = h0/b grows. There is no data.
dependence: None: the mice are independent. A cage effect or an infection breaks this assumption.
method: Independent draws of T by inversion of the survival function. The estimators are a sample mean and a fraction. The alternatives use the same uniform numbers.
diagnostics: The mean e^η E1(η)/b and the survival function give exact references: 813.8, 913.0 and 930.2 days, and P(T > 1000) = 0.127, 0.356 and 0.424. A halved initial hazard adds about log(2)/b ≈ 100 days to the mean. It moves the survival curve by one doubling time of the hazard. Other candidate models: the Gompertz–Makeham law with a constant term, and the logistic hazard, which levels off at old ages.
interpretation: The 15 % slower ageing gives the larger gain, about 116 days against about 99 days, and more mice past 1,000 days. A real study measures the effect with a sample, not with the exact law. Reject the model if the log hazard of the control group is not linear in age, for example if it levels off at old ages.

dsl:
title: Which anti-ageing intervention to take forward in mice?
problem: A laboratory tests two interventions in mice. One halves the initial hazard. The other slows the growth of the hazard by 15 %. Find the intervention with the larger gain in mean lifespan, and compare the survival to 1,000 days.
param h0 = 0.000014 {per day} "initial hazard"
param b = log(2)/100 {per day} "growth rate of the hazard: it doubles every 100 days"
param fh = 1 "factor on the initial hazard"
param fb = 1 "factor on the growth rate"
T ~ gompertz(eta = fh*h0/(fb*b), b = fb*b) {days} "lifespan of a mouse"
mean life = T {days} "mean lifespan"
prob old = T > 1000 "the mouse lives more than 1,000 days"
alt "Control": fh = 1; fb = 1
alt "Initial hazard halved": fh = 0.5; fb = 1
alt "Growth rate 15 % lower": fh = 1; fb = 0.85
maximise life
focus T

title: Which price for a life annuity sold to 100 people aged 65?
decision: Decision: the loading on the expected present value of a life annuity sold to 100 people aged 65. Estimated quantity: P(the present value of the group is more than the premiums).
reason: Adult mortality from age 30 to age 95 is close to the Gompertz law. Actuaries use Gompertz and Gompertz–Makeham laws for annuity values. The present value of a continuous annuity of 1 for each year is (1 − e^(−δT))/δ.
inputs: A hazard of 0.01 per year at age 65 and b = 0.1 per year are illustrative values. They give a mean remaining life of about 20.1 years. The force of interest δ = 0.03 is also illustrative. The expected present value of 14.42 comes from the integral of e^(−δt) S(t). There is no data.
dependence: The 100 lives are independent in this model. A common improvement of mortality, the longevity risk, makes all lives longer together. This model does not have that risk, so it understates the risk of the insurer.
method: Independent draws of 100 lifetimes. The estimators are a sample mean and a fraction. The alternatives use the same draws.
diagnostics: The page gives no reference, because T repeats. The expected present value for one life is 14.42 by quadrature, and the estimate is about 14.43. Its standard deviation is 5.29, so the group mean has a standard deviation of about 0.53. Other candidate models: the Gompertz–Makeham law, and a model with a random trend of mortality.
interpretation: A loading of 7 % is the smallest of these loadings that keeps the chance of a loss below 5 %, at about 2.5 %. A loading of 5 % gives a loss in about 8.3 % of groups. The loading falls as 1/√n for a larger group of independent lives, but not for the common longevity risk. Reject the model if the hazards of the group do not grow by a near-constant factor each year.

dsl:
title: Which price for a life annuity sold to 100 people aged 65?
problem: An insurer sells a life annuity to 100 people aged 65. The annuity pays 1 currency unit per year, continuously, until death. Find the smallest loading on the expected present value that keeps the chance of a loss on the group below 5 %.
param h65 = 0.01 {per year} "hazard at age 65"
param b = 0.1 {per year} "growth rate of the hazard"
param delta = 0.03 {per year} "force of interest"
param loading = 0.07 "loading on the expected present value"
param epv = 14.42 {currency units} "expected present value of the annuity for one life"
T ~ gompertz(eta = h65/b, b = b) repeat 100 {years} "remaining life of each annuitant"
pv := (1 - exp(-delta*T[1]))/delta {currency units} "present value for one annuitant"
group := mean((1 - exp(-delta*T))/delta) {currency units} "mean present value in the group"
mean one = pv {currency units} "expected present value for one life"
prob loss = group > (1 + loading)*epv "the group costs more than the premiums"
mean premium = (1 + loading)*epv {currency units} "premium for one life"
alt "Loading 3 %": loading = 0.03
alt "Loading 5 %": loading = 0.05
alt "Loading 7 %": loading = 0.07
alt "Loading 9 %": loading = 0.09
minimise premium
require loss <= 0.05
focus pv

title: How many care places for a cohort after 3 years?
decision: Decision: the number of long-term care places for a cohort after 3 years. Estimated quantity: P(the survivors are more than the places), the mean number of survivors, and the care-years in the 3 years.
reason: The hazard of death at old ages grows by a near-constant factor each year, as the Gompertz law states. The number of survivors after 3 years is then binomial with the probability S(3).
inputs: The cohort has 200 people aged 80 who need care now. A hazard of 0.25 per year at entry and b = 0.1 per year are illustrative values. They give S(3) = 0.417. The planner accepts a 5 % risk of too few places. There is no data.
dependence: The 200 lives are independent in this model. An epidemic or a heat wave breaks this assumption, because it raises the hazard of all residents together. New people who enter care are not in this cohort.
method: Independent draws of 200 lifetimes, then the count of survivors and the sum of min(T, 3). The estimators are a fraction and sample means.
diagnostics: The page gives no reference, because T repeats. An exact check: the survivors are Binomial(200, 0.417). This gives a mean of 83.4 and P(more than 90, 95 and 100) = 0.154, 0.042 and 0.0074. The care-years have the exact mean 200 ∫_0^3 S(t) dt = 408.6. Other candidate models: the Gompertz–Makeham law, and a frailty model with a random hazard factor for each person.
interpretation: 95 places meet the 5 % risk, with P(too few) about 0.042. 90 places are too few in about 15 % of runs. The cohort uses about 409 care-years in the 3 years. Reject the model if the deaths in the first year differ much from 200(1 − S(1)) ≈ 46. Also reject it if the health of the residents differs much.

dsl:
title: How many care places for a cohort after 3 years?
problem: A district has 200 people aged 80 who need long-term care now. Plan the care places that this cohort needs after 3 years, and the care-years in these 3 years.
param n = 200 "people in the cohort"
param h80 = 0.25 {per year} "hazard of death at age 80 in this population"
param b = 0.1 {per year} "growth rate of the hazard"
param places = 95 "care places planned for year 3"
T ~ gompertz(eta = h80/b, b = b) repeat 200 {years} "remaining life of each person"
alive := sum(T > 3) {people} "people alive after 3 years"
prob short = alive > places "the planned places are too few"
mean survivors = alive {people} "mean number alive after 3 years"

alt "90 places": places = 90
alt "95 places": places = 95
alt "100 places": places = 100
mean planned = places "places planned"
minimise planned
require short <= 0.05
focus alive

title: A hazard that rises and then falls
observe: For α = 1 and β = 3, the hazard rises to a maximum at x = 2^(1/3) ≈ 1.26 and then falls. The chance to fail in the next 0.5 time units is 0.286 at the age 0.25. It is 0.543 at the age 1 and 0.362 at the age 3. The run gives about the same values. A unit that is alive at the age 3 is thus safer than a unit at the age 1. The Weibull law cannot show this, because its hazard is monotone.
dsl:
title: A hazard that rises and then falls
problem: For β > 1 the log-logistic hazard rises to a maximum and then falls. Compare the chance to fail in the next 0.5 time units at an early, a middle and a late age.
param alpha = 1 "scale, the median"
param beta = 3 "shape"
param h = 0.5 "length of the next interval"
X ~ loglogistic(alpha = alpha, beta = beta) "time to failure"
ratio early = E[(X > 0.25)*(X <= 0.25 + h)] / E[X > 0.25] "P(fail in the next interval | alive at 0.25)"
ratio middle = E[(X > 1)*(X <= 1 + h)] / E[X > 1] "P(fail in the next interval | alive at 1)"
ratio late = E[(X > 3)*(X <= 3 + h)] / E[X > 3] "P(fail in the next interval | alive at 3)"
focus X

title: A transfer budget that closes the poverty gap
decision: Decision: the yearly budget of a cash transfer that lifts each poor household to the poverty line. Estimated quantity: the headcount ratio P(X < z) and the poverty gap per household E[max(z − X, 0)].
reason: The Fisk (log-logistic) law is a standard model of household income. Its Gini coefficient is 1/β, so one shape parameter sets the inequality. The poverty gap depends on the lower part of the law, which the median α and the shape β set.
inputs: The unit of the income X is k$ per year. The median income is α = 30. The shape is β = 3, which gives a Gini coefficient of 0.33. The poverty line is z = 18, which is 60 % of the median. There are 100,000 households. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: the incomes of households are independent in this model. The model ignores a change of behaviour that the transfer can cause.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The headcount estimator is a fraction of replicates. The gap estimator is a sample mean of max(z − X, 0). This value is between 0 and z.
diagnostics: The headcount ratio has a closed-form reference, 1/(1 + (α/z)^β). The page computes the gap by quadrature. For β = 3 the headcount is 0.178 and the gap is 0.868 k$ per household. All moments of max(z − X, 0) exist, because it is between 0 and z. Other candidate models: the lognormal law, the Singh–Maddala (Burr XII) law and the Dagum law.
interpretation: For a Gini coefficient of 0.33, 17.8 % of households are poor, and the transfer costs 86.8 M$ per year. With β = 2.5 (Gini 0.40) the cost is 124 M$, and with β = 4 (Gini 0.25) it is 43.6 M$. Thus the budget depends strongly on the inequality, at the same median. Reject the model if household survey data show a lower tail that the Fisk law does not fit, for example many zero incomes.
dsl:
title: A transfer budget that closes the poverty gap
problem: A government plans a transfer that brings each household below the poverty line up to the line. Estimate the share of poor households and the yearly cost.
param alpha = 30 {k$ per year} "median household income"
param beta = 3 "shape; the Gini coefficient is 1/β"
param z = 18 {k$ per year} "poverty line, 60 % of the median"
param households = 100000 {households}
X ~ loglogistic(alpha = alpha, beta = beta) {k$ per year} "income of one household"
prob poor = X < z "headcount ratio"
mean gap = max(z - X, 0) {k$ per household} "poverty gap per household"
mean budget = (households/1000)*max(z - X, 0) {M$ per year} "cost of the perfectly targeted transfer"
alt "Gini 0.40 (β = 2.5)": beta = 2.5
alt "Gini 0.33 (β = 3)": beta = 3
alt "Gini 0.25 (β = 4)": beta = 4
focus X

title: When to refer a patient who has not recovered after surgery
decision: Decision: the day d after surgery at which a patient who has not recovered goes to a specialist clinic. Estimated quantity: the chance to recover in the next 7 days, for a patient who has not recovered at day d. Also the mean time to recovery or referral E[min(X, d)].
reason: The chance to recover first rises as the wound heals, and then falls for patients with a complication. The log-logistic law has this hazard shape for β > 1. It is a standard accelerated failure time model in survival analysis.
inputs: The time to recovery X is in days. The median is α = 14 days and the shape is β = 2.5. Thus the hazard is largest near day 16.5. The clinic wants to refer only patients whose chance to recover in the next 7 days without help is at most 0.35. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: patients are independent. The model has no covariates. A real study adds the age of the patient and the type of surgery.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The conditional chance is a ratio estimator: the fraction of replicates that recover in (d, d + 7], over the fraction alive at d. The mean is a sample mean of min(X, d).
diagnostics: The page computes the references by quadrature. The chance to recover in the next 7 days is 0.467 at day 14 and 0.436 at day 21. It is 0.388 at day 28 and 0.344 at day 35. This chance falls after the peak of the hazard. Other candidate models: the Weibull law, whose hazard cannot rise and then fall, and the lognormal law.
interpretation: Only day 35 meets the limit of 0.35. At day 35, the clinic refers 9.2 % of patients, and the mean time to recovery or referral is 16.2 days. An earlier day refers patients who still have a good chance to recover alone. Reject the model if a Kaplan–Meier estimate from recovery records shows a monotone hazard.
dsl:
title: When to refer a patient who has not recovered after surgery
problem: Patients who have not recovered at day d go to a specialist clinic. Refer early, but only when the chance to recover in the next week without help is small.
param alpha = 14 {days} "median time to recovery"
param beta = 2.5 "shape"
param d = 21 {days} "day of the referral"
X ~ loglogistic(alpha = alpha, beta = beta) {days} "time to recovery"
prob referred = X > d "share of patients referred"
ratio next_week = E[(X > d)*(X <= d + 7)] / E[X > d] "P(recover in the next 7 days | not recovered at day d)"
mean wait = min(X, d) {days} "time to recovery or referral"
alt "Day 14": d = 14
alt "Day 21": d = 21
alt "Day 28": d = 28
alt "Day 35": d = 35
minimise wait
require next_week <= 0.35
focus X

title: A time limit for video sessions
decision: Decision: the time limit T after which the service ends a free video session. Estimated quantity: the share of sessions that the limit cuts P(X > T), and the mean number of open sessions, which sets the server capacity. At most 2 % of sessions may be cut.
reason: Session durations have a power-law tail, and the log-logistic law is a common model of call and session holding times. For β ≤ 2 the variance is infinite, so a few very long sessions use a large part of the server time.
inputs: The duration X is in minutes. The median is α = 12 minutes and the shape is β = 1.8. Thus the mean is finite but the variance is infinite. Sessions start at a rate of 50 per minute. At most 2 % of sessions may be cut. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: session durations are independent. By Little's law, the mean number of open sessions is the start rate times the mean held time E[min(X, T)].
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The share is a fraction of replicates. The load and the saved time are sample means. The objective is the smallest load that meets the limit on cut sessions.
diagnostics: P(X > T) = 1/(1 + (T/α)^β) is exact. The page computes the load by quadrature. The saved time max(X − T, 0) has a finite mean but an infinite variance for β ≤ 2, so the page shows no interval for it. Without a limit, the mean duration is απ/β / sin(π/β) ≈ 21.3 min, and the load is about 1,063 sessions. Other candidate models: the lognormal law and Pareto II.
interpretation: T = 60 min cuts 5.2 % of sessions, which is too many. T = 120 min cuts 1.6 % of sessions, and the mean load is 945 open sessions. T = 240 min cuts only 0.45 % but gives a load of 995 sessions. Thus T = 120 min saves about 2.4 min of server time per session, which is about 11 % of the mean duration. Reject the model if a log–log plot of the survival function of real durations is not straight in the tail.
dsl:
title: A time limit for video sessions
problem: A free video service ends each session after T minutes. Cut few sessions but save server time.
param alpha = 12 {min} "median session duration"
param beta = 1.8 "shape; the variance is infinite for β ≤ 2"
param rate = 50 {sessions per min} "start rate of sessions"
param T = 120 {min} "time limit"
X ~ loglogistic(alpha = alpha, beta = beta) {min} "duration that the user wants"
prob cut = X > T "share of sessions that the limit cuts"
mean saved = max(X - T, 0) {min per session} "server time saved"
mean load = rate*min(X, T) {sessions} "mean number of open sessions (Little's law)"
alt "T = 60 min": T = 60
alt "T = 120 min": T = 120
alt "T = 240 min": T = 240
minimise load
require cut <= 0.02
focus X

title: The same tail at every scale
observe: For x_m = 1 and α = 1.2, P(X > 2t)/P(X > t) = 2^(−1.2) ≈ 0.435 at every level t. The run gives about 0.435 for t = 2, 0.434 for t = 20 and 0.43 for t = 200. The interval for t = 200 is wider, because fewer values pass 200. On the tail plot, the log–log survival function is a straight line with the slope −1.2.
dsl:
title: The same tail at every scale
problem: The Pareto I tail has no scale. Doubling a level divides the tail probability by the same factor 2^α at every level.
param xm = 1 "least value"
param alpha = 1.2 "tail index"
X ~ pareto1(xm = xm, alpha = alpha)
ratio r2 = E[X > 4] / E[X > 2] "P(X > 4)/P(X > 2)"
ratio r20 = E[X > 40] / E[X > 20] "P(X > 40)/P(X > 20)"
ratio r200 = E[X > 400] / E[X > 200] "P(X > 400)/P(X > 200)"
focus X

title: A wealth tax threshold for a revenue target
decision: Decision: the threshold t of a 2 % yearly tax on net wealth above t. Estimated quantity: the revenue τ N E[max(X − t, 0)] and the number of taxed households N P(X > t). The revenue must be at least 2,000 M$ per year.
reason: The top of the wealth distribution follows a Pareto law with good accuracy. Pareto I describes wealth above a high lower limit x_m. The tax base above t depends only on the tail index α.
inputs: Wealth X is in M$. The model covers N = 200,000 households with a wealth of at least x_m = 1 M$. The tail index is α = 1.5. The tax rate is τ = 2 %. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: households are independent. The model ignores avoidance, which reduces the base, and a change of wealth over time.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The estimators are sample means and a fraction of replicates.
diagnostics: The number of taxed households has the reference N (t/x_m)^(−α). The revenue has the exact value τ N x_m^α t^(1 − α)/(α − 1) for α > 1. The page has no reference for the revenue. Its variance is infinite for α ≤ 2, so its interval is not reliable, and a run usually gives less than the exact value. The very rich households, which pay most of the tax, are rare in a run. Other candidate models: Pareto II and the generalised Pareto law above a threshold.
interpretation: The exact revenue is 3,578, 2,530, 1,789 and 1,131 M$ per year for t = 5, 10, 20 and 50 M$. Thus t = 10 M$ meets the target and taxes 6,325 households. A run of 2^18 households gave about 2,340 M$ for t = 10 M$, below the exact value. Use the exact formula for the decision, and use the run only as a check. Reject the model if a Pareto quantile plot of tax or rich-list data is not straight above x_m.
dsl:
title: A wealth tax threshold for a revenue target
problem: A 2 % yearly tax applies to the part of net wealth above a threshold t. Raise at least 2,000 M$ per year and tax as few households as possible.
param xm = 1 {M$} "least wealth in the model"
param alpha = 1.5 "tail index of wealth"
param households = 200000 {households} "households with a wealth of at least x_m"
param tau = 0.02 "tax rate"
param t = 10 {M$} "threshold"
X ~ pareto1(xm = xm, alpha = alpha) {M$} "net wealth of one household"
mean revenue = tau*households*max(X - t, 0) {M$ per year}
mean taxed = households*(X > t) {households}
alt "t = 5 M$": t = 5
alt "t = 10 M$": t = 10
alt "t = 20 M$": t = 20
alt "t = 50 M$": t = 50
minimise taxed
require revenue >= 2000
focus X

title: A policy limit for data-breach costs
decision: Decision: the policy limit L for the notification cost of a data breach. Estimated quantity: the expected payment per breach E[min(cX, L)], and the probability P(cX > L) that a breach uses all of the limit. At most 0.5 % of breaches may use all of the limit.
reason: Some studies of breach records find a Pareto tail with an index below 1 (Maillart and Sornette, Physica A, 2010). This model uses α = 0.7. For α < 1 the mean of X is infinite. Thus the price of the cover exists only because of the limit, and it grows without bound with L.
inputs: X is the number of records in a breach, at least x_m = 1,000 records. The tail index is α = 0.7. The cost is c = 2 $ per record. The limits are 1, 5 and 20 M$. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: one breach. The real cost per record falls with the size of the breach, which this linear cost ignores.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The payment estimator is a sample mean of a bounded value, so its variance is finite. The exhaustion estimator is a fraction of replicates.
diagnostics: The page computes the references by quadrature. The exact form is E[min(X, M)] = x_m(1 + ((M/x_m)^(1 − α) − 1)/(1 − α)), with M = L/c. Without the limit, the expected payment is infinite. Other candidate models: a lognormal law, a truncated Pareto law with a finite upper limit, and Pareto II.
interpretation: 1.3 % of breaches use all of L = 1 M$, which is too often. 0.42 % of breaches use all of L = 5 M$, and its pure premium is 65,000 $ per breach. L = 20 M$ costs 101,000 $ per breach. The premium grows as L^(1 − α) = L^0.3 and has no upper bound. Reject the model if breach records above x_m show a tail that bends down on a log–log plot.
dsl:
title: A policy limit for data-breach costs
problem: A cyber policy pays the notification cost of a breach, up to a limit L. The records lost in a breach have a Pareto tail with an infinite mean. Choose the cheapest limit that few breaches use up.
param xm = 1000 {records} "least breach size in the model"
param alpha = 0.7 "tail index; the mean is infinite for α ≤ 1"
param cost = 2 {$ per record} "notification cost"
param L = 5000000 {$} "policy limit"
X ~ pareto1(xm = xm, alpha = alpha) {records} "records in one breach"
mean payment = cost*min(X, L/cost) {$ per breach} "expected payment, the pure premium"
prob exhaust = cost*X > L "the breach uses all of the limit"
alt "L = 1 M$": L = 1000000
alt "L = 5 M$": L = 5000000
alt "L = 20 M$": L = 20000000
minimise payment
require exhaust <= 0.005
focus X

title: How much of a fire season is one fire?
decision: Decision: the share r of the seasonal suppression budget that a fire agency keeps in reserve for the largest fire. Estimated quantity: P(the largest fire needs more than the reserve) = P(max(X)/sum(X) > r). Also the unused reserve E[max(r − max(X)/sum(X), 0)].
reason: Burned areas of wildfires have a power-law tail with an index often below 1. For α < 1 the share of the largest fire does not tend to 0 as the number of fires grows: E[sum/max] tends to 1/(1 − α). Pareto I is the simplest law with this tail above a least size.
inputs: A season has 100 fires, each with a burned area of at least x_m = 10 ha. The tail index is α = 0.7. The cost to fight a fire is proportional to its burned area. The reserve may be too small in at most 25 % of seasons. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: the fires are independent, and the model uses a constant number of fires. Real fires in one season share the weather, which makes large fires come together.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform, 100 for each season. The estimators are a fraction of seasons and a sample mean.
diagnostics: P(max(X) > 100,000 ha) = 1 − (1 − (10^4)^(−0.7))^100 = 0.147 is an exact reference. The share max(X)/sum(X) is between 0 and 1, so all its moments exist, but the page has no reference for it. For α < 1, a theorem of Bingham and Teugels gives E[sum/max] → 1/(1 − α) ≈ 3.3 as the number of fires grows. Thus the largest fire stays a large share of the season. For α > 1, max/sum tends to 0. Other candidate models: a truncated Pareto law with the largest possible fire size, and a lognormal law.
interpretation: The largest fire is about 48 % of the season on average. It is more than half of the season with a probability of about 0.41. A reserve of r = 0.7 is too small in about 22 % of seasons, and r = 0.8 in about 15 %. r = 0.7 meets the limit with the least unused reserve. Reject the model if the largest fires of past seasons are a much smaller share of the burned area.
dsl:
title: How much of a fire season is one fire?
problem: A fire agency keeps a share r of its seasonal budget for the largest fire. With a tail index below 1, one fire can be a large part of the season.
param xm = 10 {ha} "least burned area in the model"
param alpha = 0.7 "tail index"
param r = 0.5 "reserve share of the budget"
X ~ pareto1(xm = xm, alpha = alpha) repeat 100 {ha} "burned areas of the fires of a season"
share := max(X)/sum(X) "share of the largest fire"
prob short = share > r "the largest fire needs more than the reserve"
mean unused = max(r - share, 0) "unused reserve, as a share of the budget"
M := max(X) {ha} "the largest fire"
mean expected_share = share "E[max/sum]"
prob huge = M > 100000 "a fire larger than 100,000 ha"
alt "r = 0.5": r = 0.5
alt "r = 0.7": r = 0.7
alt "r = 0.8": r = 0.8
minimise unused
require short <= 0.25
focus share

title: One big jump makes a large sum
observe: The 10 values are Pareto II with σ = 1 and α = 1.5, so the mean of the sum S is 20. At x = 300, P(M > x) = 0.00191 and 10 P(X > x) = 0.00191 (exact references). The run gives P(S > x) ≈ 0.0022, near these values. About 91 % of the sums above 300 have one value above 300: one big jump makes the large sum. At x = 20, which is only the mean of S, P(S > x) ≈ 0.26 is far from P(M > x) = 0.099. Only about 39 % of these sums have a value above 20. The approximation P(S > x) ≈ n P(X > x) is a limit as x → ∞, and its convergence is slow.
dsl:
title: One big jump makes a large sum
problem: For a subexponential law, a large sum of 10 values comes from one large value. Then P(S > x) ≈ P(M > x) ≈ 10 P(X > x) for a large x.
param sigma = 1 "scale"
param alpha = 1.5 "tail index"
param x = 300 "large level"
X ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) repeat 10 "10 independent values"
Y ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) "one value"
S := sum(X) "sum"
M := max(X) "maximum"
prob sum_big = S > x "P(S > x)"
prob max_big = M > x "P(M > x)"
mean ten_one = 10*(Y > x) "10 P(X > x)"
ratio one_jump = E[(M > x)*(S > x)] / E[S > x] "P(M > x | S > x)"
alt "x = 20": x = 20
alt "x = 300": x = 300
focus S

title: Price an excess-of-loss reinsurance layer
decision: Decision: the priority d of a reinsurance layer that pays 5,000 k€ in excess of d for each claim. Estimated quantity: the layer loss per claim E[min(max(X − d, 0), L)], the premium, and the retained loss per claim. The premium must be at most 8,000 k€ per year.
reason: Large property claims have a power-law tail, and reinsurers price layers with Pareto laws. Pareto II also follows from a gamma mixture of exponential claim sizes over a varied portfolio. The mean excess over d grows linearly in d.
inputs: The claim X is in k€. The scale is σ = 100 k€ and the tail index is α = 1.8, so the mean is 125 k€ and the variance is infinite. There are 400 claims per year. The layer limit is L = 5,000 k€. The premium loading is 30 %. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: claims are independent. One event that causes many claims breaks this assumption. Then the insurer needs an event cover.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The estimators are sample means. The layer loss is between 0 and L, so its variance is finite. The mean claim does not change with d, so the most cover (the largest layer loss) within the budget gives the smallest retained loss.
diagnostics: The page computes the references by quadrature. The exact layer loss is σ/(α − 1) ((1 + d/σ)^(1 − α) − (1 + (d + L)/σ)^(1 − α)). The retained loss has an infinite variance for α ≤ 2, so its interval is not reliable. Its exact mean is 125 k€ minus the layer loss. Other candidate models: the generalised Pareto law above a threshold, the lognormal law and Burr XII.
interpretation: The premium is 12,906 k€ for d = 500 k€. It is 7,121 k€ for d = 1,000 k€ and 3,543 k€ for d = 2,000 k€. Thus d = 1,000 k€ is the lowest priority within the budget. Then 1.3 % of claims reach the layer, and the insurer keeps 111.3 k€ of the mean claim of 125 k€. Reject the model if the mean excess plot of large claims is not near a straight line.
dsl:
title: Price an excess-of-loss reinsurance layer
problem: An insurer buys a layer that pays the part of each claim between d and d + L. A lower priority d gives more cover but costs more. Choose d within the premium budget.
param sigma = 100 {k€} "scale of the claim size"
param alpha = 1.8 "tail index"
param claims = 400 {claims per year}
param L = 5000 {k€} "layer limit"
param load = 0.3 "premium loading"
param d = 1000 {k€} "priority"
X ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) {k€} "size of one claim"
layer := min(max(X - d, 0), L) {k€} "the part of the claim that the layer pays"
mean layer_loss = layer {k€ per claim}
mean premium = (1 + load)*claims*layer {k€ per year}
mean retained = X - layer {k€ per claim} "the part of the claim that the insurer keeps"
prob hit = X > d "the claim reaches the layer"
alt "d = 500 k€": d = 500
alt "d = 1,000 k€": d = 1000
alt "d = 2,000 k€": d = 2000
maximise layer_loss
require premium <= 8000
focus X

title: How large a file to keep in an edge cache
decision: Decision: the size limit B of files that an edge cache stores. Estimated quantity: the share of requested bytes that the cache serves, E[X·1(X ≤ B)]/E[X]. Also the memory for 1,000,000 files. The memory must be at most 70 GB.
reason: Some measurements of web traffic find file sizes with a power-law tail and an index between 1 and 1.5 (Crovella and Bestavros, 1997). Pareto II is a heavy-tailed law of sizes from 0 up. With α near 1, a few large files hold a large share of the bytes.
inputs: The size X is in kB. The scale is σ = 20 kB and the tail index is α = 1.2, so the mean is 100 kB and the variance is infinite. Users request each of the 1,000,000 files with the same probability. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: file sizes are independent. Real requests prefer some files, so a model of popularity (for example the Zipf law) changes the result.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The byte share is a sample mean of X·1(X ≤ B), divided by the exact mean E[X] = σ/(α − 1). This value has the bound B, so its variance is finite. The ratio of two sample means would be very noisy, because X has an infinite variance. The memory is a sample mean of the same value.
diagnostics: The page computes the references by quadrature. A cache of files up to 1 MB stores 99.1 % of the files but serves only 45.5 % of the bytes. Other candidate models: the lognormal law for the body with a Pareto tail, and Pareto I.
interpretation: B = 10 MB serves 65.4 % of the bytes with 65.4 GB of memory. B = 100 MB serves 78.2 % but needs 78.2 GB, which is more than 70 GB. The last 0.06 % of the files hold about a third of the bytes. Reject the model if a log–log plot of the size distribution of the real catalogue is not straight in the tail.
dsl:
title: How large a file to keep in an edge cache
problem: An edge cache stores each file that is not larger than B. A larger B serves more bytes but needs more memory.
param sigma = 20 {kB} "scale of the file size"
param alpha = 1.2 "tail index"
param files = 1000000 {files}
param B = 10000 {kB} "largest file that the cache stores"
X ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) {kB} "size of one file"
prob stored = X <= B "share of files that the cache stores"
mean byte_share = (alpha - 1)/sigma*min(X, B)*(X <= B) "share of requested bytes that the cache serves, X·1(X ≤ B)/E[X]"
mean memory = files/1000000*min(X, B)*(X <= B) {GB} "memory of the cache"
alt "B = 1 MB": B = 1000
alt "B = 10 MB": B = 10000
alt "B = 100 MB": B = 100000
maximise byte_share
require memory <= 70
focus X

title: When to send a reminder to a customer who has not come back
decision: Decision: the day r after a purchase at which a shop sends a reminder to a customer who has not come back. Estimated quantity: the share of wasted reminders, which go to customers who come back in the next 30 days without them. Also the share of customers who get a reminder.
reason: The model assumes that each customer comes back after an exponential time with a personal rate, and that the rates differ between customers. If the rates have a gamma law, the time to return has the Pareto II law. Its hazard α/(σ + x) falls with time, because the frequent customers come back first.
inputs: The time X is in days. The rates have a gamma law with the shape α = 2 and the scale 1/σ, with σ = 60 days. Thus the mean time to return is 60 days. At most 30 % of the reminders can go to waste. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: customers are independent. The model ignores customers who never come back. A Pareto/NBD model adds them.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The wasted share is a ratio estimator. The reach is a fraction of replicates.
diagnostics: The wasted share is 1 − ((σ + r)/(σ + r + 30))^α, and the reach is ((σ + r)/σ)^(−α). The page computes them by quadrature and in closed form. Other candidate models: the exponential law with one rate for all customers, and the Pareto/NBD model.
interpretation: The wasted share is 0.44 at day 30, 0.36 at day 60, 0.31 at day 90 and 0.27 at day 120. Only day 120 meets the limit of 0.3, and then 11 % of customers get a reminder. With one rate for all customers, the wasted share does not change with r, and no day would be better. Reject the model if the return hazard of real customers does not fall with time.
dsl:
title: When to send a reminder to a customer who has not come back
problem: A shop sends a reminder to each customer who has not come back r days after a purchase. A reminder is wasted if the customer comes back in the next 30 days without it.
param sigma = 60 {days} "scale"
param alpha = 2 "shape of the gamma law of the rates"
param r = 60 {days} "day of the reminder"
X ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) {days} "time to the next purchase"
prob reach = X > r "share of customers who get a reminder"
ratio wasted = E[(X > r)*(X <= r + 30)] / E[X > r] "P(come back in the next 30 days | not back at day r)"
alt "Day 30": r = 30
alt "Day 60": r = 60
alt "Day 90": r = 90
alt "Day 120": r = 120
maximise reach
require wasted <= 0.3
focus X

title: Two shapes: the body and the tail
observe: The three laws have ck = 3, so their tails decay as x^(−3). The ratio P(X > 10)/P(X > 5) is 0.162 for c = 1, 0.126 for c = 3 and 0.125 for c = 6. For c = 3 and c = 6 they are near the limit 2^(−3) = 0.125. For c = 1 the ratio at these levels is still far from its limit. The bodies differ much: P(X ≤ 0.5) is 0.704, 0.111 and 0.0077. The means are 0.50, 1.21 and 1.40. On the tail plot, the three curves become parallel lines on the right.
dsl:
title: Two shapes: the body and the tail
problem: In Burr XII, c sets the body near 0 and the product ck sets the tail index. Compare three laws with ck = 3 and different c.
param c = 3 "first shape, the body"
param k = 1 "second shape"
param lambda = 1 "scale"
X ~ burr12(c = c, k = k, lambda = lambda)
prob small = X <= 0.5 "the body: P(X ≤ 0.5)"
mean m = X "mean"
ratio tail = E[X > 10] / E[X > 5] "P(X > 10)/P(X > 5), near 2^(−ck) = 0.125"
alt "c = 1, k = 3": c = 1; k = 3
alt "c = 3, k = 1": c = 3; k = 1
alt "c = 6, k = 0.5": c = 6; k = 0.5
focus X

title: A taper rate for a housing allowance
decision: Decision: the taper rate r of a housing allowance max(A − rX, 0), with A = 8 k$ per year. Estimated quantity: the share of households that get the allowance P(X < A/r), and the mean cost per household E[max(A − rX, 0)]. The cost must be at most 1 k$ per household.
reason: The Singh–Maddala (Burr XII) law fits household income well over the whole range. It has one shape for the lower part and the tail index ck for the top. The allowance depends on the lower part, which a one-shape law fits less well.
inputs: The income X is in k$ per year. The shapes are c = 2.8 and k = 1.4, and the scale is λ = 50 k$. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: households are independent. The model ignores a change of work hours that the taper can cause.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The estimators are a fraction of replicates and a sample mean of a bounded value.
diagnostics: P(X < A/r) has a closed-form reference, and the page computes the cost by quadrature. The cost is between 0 and A, so all its moments exist. The median income of the model is 42.6 k$ and the mean is 49.0 k$. Other candidate models: the Fisk (log-logistic) law, the Dagum law and the lognormal law.
interpretation: r = 0.25 reaches 29.7 % of households at a cost of 0.708 k$ per household. r = 0.2 reaches 45.1 % but costs 1.17 k$, which is more than the limit. Reject the model if survey incomes show a lower part that differs from the fitted law, for example a large atom at 0.
dsl:
title: A taper rate for a housing allowance
problem: A housing allowance pays A − rX to a household with income X, and 0 when this is negative. A lower taper r reaches more households but costs more.
param c = 2.8 "first shape"
param k = 1.4 "second shape"
param lambda = 50 {k$ per year} "scale"
param A = 8 {k$ per year} "allowance at zero income"
param r = 0.25 "taper rate"
X ~ burr12(c = c, k = k, lambda = lambda) {k$ per year} "income of one household"
prob reach = X < A/r "share of households that get the allowance"
mean cost = r*max(A/r - X, 0) {k$ per household}
alt "r = 0.4": r = 0.4
alt "r = 0.25": r = 0.25
alt "r = 0.2": r = 0.2
maximise reach
require cost <= 1
focus X

title: A deductible for motor damage claims
decision: Decision: the deductible d of a motor damage policy. Estimated quantity: the reduction of the pure premium E[min(X, d)]/E[X]. Also the share of claims that the deductible removes, P(X ≤ d). The premium must fall by at least 25 %.
reason: Motor damage claims have many small amounts, a mode above 0 and a moderately heavy tail. Burr XII fits these claim sizes well, because c sets the body and ck sets the tail.
inputs: The claim X is in $. The shapes are c = 1.5 and k = 2, so the tail index is 3. The scale is λ = 2,000 $. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: claims are independent. A deductible also stops policyholders from reporting some small claims. This model ignores that effect.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The reduction is a ratio estimator. The removed share is a fraction of replicates.
diagnostics: The page computes E[min(X, d)] by quadrature, and the mean claim is 1,612 $. The ratio has no reference, but the exact values are 0.150, 0.282 and 0.488 for d = 250, 500 and 1,000 $. Other candidate models: the lognormal law, the gamma law and Pareto II.
interpretation: d = 500 $ cuts the pure premium by 28 %, and the policyholder pays 455 $ of each claim on average. The deductible removes 21 % of claims, which also saves handling costs. d = 250 $ cuts only 15 %. Reject the model if the claim amounts show many claims near the old deductible, which shows a reporting effect.
dsl:
title: A deductible for motor damage claims
problem: The policyholder pays the first d $ of each claim. Choose the smallest deductible that cuts the pure premium by at least 25 %.
param c = 1.5 "first shape"
param k = 2 "second shape"
param lambda = 2000 {$} "scale"

title: A design depth for daily rainfall
decision: Decision: the daily rainfall depth h that a storm-water tank must hold. Estimated quantity: the probability that the largest daily rainfall of a year is more than h, P(max(X) > h). It must be at most 0.1, which is a return period of 10 years.
reason: Global studies of daily rainfall on wet days find Burr XII among the best fits. It has a body near 0 and a power-law tail with the index ck, which a gamma law does not have.
inputs: X is the rainfall on one wet day, in mm. The shapes are c = 0.9 and k = 6, so the tail index is 5.4. The scale is λ = 30 mm. A year has 100 wet days. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
dependence: None: wet days are independent and the law does not change with the season. In real records, wet days come in spells, and their amounts have a correlation.
method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform, 100 for each year. The estimator is a fraction of years.
diagnostics: P(max(X) > h) = 1 − (1 − P(X > h))^100 is an exact reference. The mean rainfall of a wet day is 5.35 mm. Other candidate models: the gamma law, the generalised Pareto law above a threshold, and the GEV law for the annual maximum.
interpretation: P(the largest daily rainfall of a year > h) is 0.165 for 60 mm, 0.061 for 80 mm and 0.026 for 100 mm. Thus 80 mm is the smallest of these depths that meets the limit, with a return period of about 16 years. Reject the model if the annual maxima of the station record exceed the design depths more often than the model says.

param lambda = 30 {mm} "scale"
param h = 80 {mm} "design depth"

alt "h = 60 mm": h = 60
alt "h = 80 mm": h = 80
alt "h = 100 mm": h = 100

require over <= 0.1

title: Maxima of Pareto draws become Fréchet
observe: M is the largest of 100 Pareto I draws with x_m = 1, divided by 100^(1/α). Its exact law is P(M ≤ x) = (1 − x^(−α)/100)^100. For α = 1.5, P(M ≤ 0.5) = 0.0567 and P(M > 4) = 0.1176. The Fréchet law gives 0.0591 and 0.1175. For α = 3, P(M ≤ 0.5) = 0.00024 against 0.00034, and P(M > 4) = 0.0155 for both laws. The two laws differ most in the lower part, where n = 100 is still small. On the tail plot both curves fall with the slope −α.

title: Maxima of Pareto draws become Fréchet
problem: The largest of n Pareto draws, divided by n^(1/α), has a law near the Fréchet law with the same α.
param a = 1.5 "tail index α"
X ~ pareto1(xm = 1, alpha = a) repeat 100 "one Pareto draw"
M := max(X)/100^(1/a) "the normalised maximum of 100 draws"
F ~ frechet(alpha = a, s = 1, m = 0) "a Fréchet draw for comparison"
prob m_low = M <= 0.5 "P(M ≤ 0.5)"
prob f_low = F <= 0.5 "P(F ≤ 0.5)"
prob m_high = M > 4 "P(M > 4)"
prob f_high = F > 4 "P(F > 4)"
alt "α = 1.5": a = 1.5
alt "α = 3": a = 3
focus M

title: Retention of a cover for the largest claim of a year
decision: Decision: the retention R of a cover that pays the part of the largest claim of the year above R. Estimated quantity: the premium 1.3·E[max(M − R, 0)], the retained part E[min(M, R)] and P(M > R).
reason: Single claims of a property portfolio often have a Pareto-type tail. The maximum of many such claims is near the Fréchet law, by the Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem. The tail index α of the claims is also the tail index of the maximum.
inputs: The tail index is α = 2.5 and the scale is s = 2 million. The premium loading is 1.3, and the budget for the premium is 0.5 million per year. These values are illustrative. The model assumes many claims each year and the same claim law every year.
dependence: None inside the model: M is one value for one year. A storm that causes many large claims together changes the law of the maximum, and an aggregate cover is then a better tool.
method: Independent draws of M by the inverse transform. The estimators are sample means of min(M, R) and 1.3·max(M − R, 0), and a fraction of replicates for P(M > R). The alternatives share the streams.
diagnostics: P(M > R) has a closed form: 0.304, 0.162, 0.096 and 0.062 for R = 3, 4, 5 and 6. E[min(M, R)] has a reference by quadrature. The page shows the moment status of the premium as unknown and gives it no reference. Check it with E[max(M − R, 0)] = E[M] − E[min(M, R)]. Here E[M] = sΓ(1 − 1/α) = 2.978. This gives premiums of 0.884, 0.593, 0.430 and 0.330 million. The variance of M is finite because α > 2. Other candidate models: a GEV law with a free shape ξ, and a Gumbel law, which has a light tail.
interpretation: R = 5 million is the lowest retention whose premium fits the budget. Its premium is about 0.43 million, and the cover pays in about 1 year in 10. R = 4 costs about 0.59 million. A smaller α makes the premium much larger. Reject the model if past yearly maxima show a lighter tail on a Fréchet plot. Also reject it if the claim count changes much between years.
